citations.quote:
For all $1\le i,j\le n$ one has $X_iX_j=X_jX_i$ in $\mathbb Z[S_n]$, hence in
$R[S_n]$ for every commutative ring $R$; that is, the Jucys-Murphy elements
commute pairwise, and the subalgebra they generate is commutative.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $R$ be a commutative ring. In the group ring $R[S_n]$ of
the symmetric group on $\{1,\dots,n\}$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-symmetric-group]], [[def-group-ring]]), where $(j\ k)$ denotes the
transposition of the distinct entries $j,k\in\{1,\dots,n\}$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), the **Jucys-Murphy elements** are
$$X_1:=0,\qquad X_k:=\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}(j\ k)\in R[S_n]\qquad(2\le k\le n).$$
Each $X_k$ is a finite sum of group elements with coefficient $1$, so the
formula already defines an element of the integral group ring
$\mathbb Z[S_n]$, and its image under the base change
$\mathbb Z[S_n]\to R[S_n]$ is the displayed element
([[def-restriction-and-extension-of-scalars]]); for $1\le k\le m\le n$ the element
$X_k$ of $R[S_m]$, computed in the subgroup
$S_m=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,m\})\subseteq S_n$ of permutations fixing
$m+1,\dots,n$, maps to $X_k$ under the inclusion $S_m\hookrightarrow S_n$.
Equivalently $X_k=T_k-T_{k-1}$, where $T_k=\sum_{1\le i<j\le k}(i\ j)$ is the
sum of all transpositions in $S_k$.

Let $n\ge1$. (a) The elements $X_1,\dots,X_n$ act diagonally in the Young
basis of the previous item: for every standard tableau $T$ of size $n$ and
every $k$, $X_kv_T=c_T(k)v_T$, and the joint eigenspaces are
one-dimensional, indexed by the standard tableaux. (b) A vector
$\alpha=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in\mathbb Z^n$ occurs as the joint eigenvalue vector
of a $v_T$, equivalently $\alpha=\operatorname{Cont}(T)$ for a standard
tableau $T$, if and only if: (1) $a_1=0$; (2) for every $q>1$ at least one of
$a_q-1,a_q+1$ occurs among $a_1,\dots,a_{q-1}$; (3) if $a_p=a_q$ with $p<q$,
then both $a_p-1$ and $a_p+1$ occur among $a_{p+1},\dots,a_{q-1}$. The
association $T\mapsto\operatorname{Cont}(T)$ is a bijection from the standard
tableaux of size $n$ onto this set.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $f\in\mathbb C[y_1,\dots,y_n]$ be a symmetric polynomial.
Then (i) $f(X_1,\dots,X_n)\in Z(\mathbb C[S_n])$; and (ii) conversely, for
every central element $z\in Z(\mathbb C[S_n])$ there is a symmetric polynomial
$f$ with $z=f(X_1,\dots,X_n)$. In other words, the symmetric polynomial
evaluations of the Jucys-Murphy elements are exactly the central elements of
the symmetric group algebra.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $I_1,\ldots,I_r$ be pairwise comaximal ideals, where $r\ge1$. Then the canonical map
$$ R\longrightarrow \prod_{i=1}^r R/I_i,\qquad x\longmapsto(x+I_1,\ldots,x+I_r) $$
is surjective, its kernel is $\bigcap_{i=1}^r I_i$, and
$$ \bigcap_{i=1}^r I_i=\prod_{i=1}^r I_i. $$
Equivalently,
$$ R/\prod_{i=1}^r I_i\cong\prod_{i=1}^r R/I_i. $$

For $H\le G$, restriction forgets from $\mathbb Z[G]$ to $\mathbb Z[H]$. For a left $H$-module $M$, set $\operatorname{Ind}_H^G M=\mathbb Z[G]\otimes_{\mathbb Z[H]}M$ and $\operatorname{Coind}_H^G M=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z[H]}(\mathbb Z[G],M)$, with $G$ acting on the latter by $(g\varphi)(x)=\varphi(xg)$.
If $H\le G$ and a left (respectively right) coset transversal is supplied, then $\mathbb Z[G]$ is free as a right (respectively left) $\mathbb Z[H]$-module on it.

Fix a splitting $p$-modular system $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ for a finite group $G$.
A **$p$-block idempotent** is a primitive central idempotent of $\mathcal O G$
or, after reduction, of $kG$.

If $e$ is such an idempotent, the corresponding **block** is the two-sided
ideal

$$B=\mathcal OGe\qquad\text{or}\qquad B=kGe.$$

The primitive central idempotents are pairwise orthogonal and sum to $1$, so
the algebra splits as a direct product of its block summands.

boundaries.evidence: Step 8.1 disposes of n = 0 explicitly: the empty sequence is the only index, e(∅) = 1, and E_i is the zero functor on the zero module, so the statements are vacuous and no case is excluded.

Zero is an allowed residue and content entry: step 1.1 factors the minimal polynomial over all a in F_p including a = 0, step 2.1 keeps the exponent m_0, and step 5.1 sums over every i in Z/p including i = 0.
For n = 1 the decomposition of step 5.1 collapses to the single-node projectors P_{1,a} and E_iM = e((i))M, and the identities of steps 2.1 and 3.1 apply verbatim.

The p = 2 case is included: step 1.1 needs only that the integer minimal polynomial splits over F_p, step 7.1 uses only the idempotent decomposition, and step 8.1 records the block theorem with characteristic 2 included.
The extreme residues 0 and p − 1 are ordinary members of Z/p: the direct sum of step 5.1 runs over the whole group and step 7.1 treats every i uniformly.
Only finite index sets and finite orbit sums are selected: the construction of step 5.1 uses the finite set F_p of residues and finite orbits, and no choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: *Eigenvalues in $\mathbb F_p$.* Let $h_r\in\mathbb Q[X]$ be the minimal polynomial of $L_r$ acting on the left regular module $\mathbb QS_n$. Over $\mathbb C$ the regular module is the direct sum of the complex Specht modules with multiplicities, and by [F2] the eigenvalues of $L_r$ on that module are the integers $c_T(r)$, the contents of the node containing $r$, over all standard tableaux $T$ of $n$ nodes; hence $h_r=\prod_{a\in E_r}(X-a)$ is squarefree with the integer roots in the finite set $E_r$. Reduction of coefficients modulo $p$ gives $h_r(L_r)=0$ in $kS_n$, so the minimal polynomial $f_r$ of $L_r$ on the regular module $kS_n$ divides the reduction $\bar h_r=\prod_{a\in E_r}(X-\bar a)$ in $k[X]$, and every root of $f_r$ lies in the image $\mathbb F_p$ of $\mathbb Z$ in $k$.

*Antipode invariance.* The antipode $\sigma:kS_n\to kS_n$, $\sigma(g)=g^{-1}$, is an anti-automorphism fixing every transposition, hence fixes each $L_r$ and therefore each $P_{r,a}\in k[L_r]$ and each $e(\mathbf i)$.

*Primary projectors.* Write $f_r=\prod_{a\in\mathbb F_p}(X-a)^{m_a}$ with $m_a\ge0$. For $a\ne b$ the ideals $\big((X-a)^{m_a}\big)$ and $\big((X-b)^{m_b}\big)$ of $k[X]$ are comaximal, since two powers of distinct linear polynomials are coprime and Bezout gives $1=u(X)(X-a)^{m_a}+v(X)(X-b)^{m_b}$. By [F4] applied to the ring $k[X]/(f_r)$ and its comaximal ideals, the canonical map $k[X]/(f_r)\to\prod_{a:m_a>0}k[X]/\big((X-a)^{m_a}\big)$ is an isomorphism; let $\varepsilon_{r,a}$ be the preimage of the idempotent supported at the $a$-th factor. Then $\sum_a\varepsilon_{r,a}=1$, $\varepsilon_{r,a}^2=\varepsilon_{r,a}$, $\varepsilon_{r,a}\varepsilon_{r,b}=0$ for $a\ne b$, and $(X-a)^{m_a}\varepsilon_{r,a}=0$ in $k[X]/(f_r)$. Substituting the algebra element $L_r$ for $X$ (legitimate because $f_r(L_r)=0$) gives elements $P_{r,a}:=\varepsilon_{r,a}(L_r)\in k[L_r]$ with $\sum_aP_{r,a}=1$, $P_{r,a}P_{r,b}=\delta_{a,b}P_{r,a}$ and $(L_r-a)^{m_a}P_{r,a}=0$.

*These are the primary projections.* Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module. Since the $P_{r,a}$ are polynomials in $L_r$, they commute with $L_r$ and with one another; as $1=\sum_aP_{r,a}$ one has $M=\sum_aP_{r,a}M$, and $(L_r-a)^{m_a}$ annihilates $P_{r,a}M$, so $P_{r,a}M\subseteq M_{r,a}$. Conversely, if $m\in M_{r,a}$, then $(L_r-a)^Nm=0$ for $N\ge m_a$, and for $b\ne a$ the element $L_r-b=(a-b)+(L_r-a)$ is invertible on the $a$-primary subspace because $(a-b)\in k^\times$ and $(L_r-a)$ is nilpotent there; from $P_{r,b}(L_r-b)^{m_b}=0$ we get $P_{r,b}m=0$ for $b\ne a$, whence $m=P_{r,a}m$. Thus $P_{r,a}M=M_{r,a}$ and $M=\bigoplus_aM_{r,a}$. The products $e(\mathbf i)=\prod_rP_{r,i_r}$ are idempotent, pairwise orthogonal and sum to $1$ by multiplicativity of the $P_{r,a}$; applying the same argument successively to the commuting operators $L_1,\dots,L_n$ gives $e(\mathbf i)M=M_{\mathbf i}$.

*Centrality of the content sums.* Fix a content vector $\alpha\in(\mathbb Z/p)^n$ and an ordering $c=(c_1,\dots,c_n)$ of its entries. For every $r$ and $a$ choose a representative $q_{r,a}\in k[X]$ of the class $\varepsilon_{r,a}\in k[X]/(f_r)$, so that $P_{r,a}=q_{r,a}(L_r)$. Then, because the orbit $I_\alpha$ consists exactly of the orderings $c_\sigma=(c_{\sigma(1)},\dots,c_{\sigma(n)})$ of $c$, $$e_\alpha=\sum_{\mathbf i\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf i)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{r=1}^nq_{r,c_{\sigma(r)}}(L_r)=F(L_1,\dots,L_n),$$ where $F(y_1,\dots,y_n):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{r=1}^nq_{r,c_{\sigma(r)}}(y_r)$ is symmetric in $y_1,\dots,y_n$: permuting the variables permutes the summands, since $c$ is a fixed multiset. Lift the coefficients of the $q_{r,a}$ arbitrarily from $\mathbb F_p$ to $\mathbb Z$, obtaining $\tilde q_{r,a}\in\mathbb Z[X]$ and a symmetric $\tilde F\in\mathbb Z[y_1,\dots,y_n]$ with $F=\tilde F\bmod p$. By [F3] applied over $\mathbb C$ to $\tilde F$, the element $\tilde F(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ is central in $\mathbb C[S_n]$; it lies in $\mathbb Z[S_n]$, so the centralizer equations, being integral, hold in $\mathbb Z[S_n]$ and hence in $kS_n$ after reduction. Therefore $e_\alpha=F(L_1,\dots,L_n)$ is central in $kS_n$. It is idempotent because the $e(\mathbf i)$ for $\mathbf i\in I_\alpha$ are pairwise orthogonal idempotents, so $e_\alpha^2=\sum_{\mathbf i,\mathbf i'}e(\mathbf i)e(\mathbf i')=e_\alpha$, and distinct content sums are orthogonal by the same orthogonality.

*The functor projectors.* Fix $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and a content vector $\alpha\in(\mathbb Z/p)^{n-1}$ with ordering $c$. Expanding the orbit sum, $$e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=\sum_{\mathbf j\in I_\alpha}e((\mathbf j,i))=\Bigl(\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n-1}}\prod_{r=1}^{n-1}q_{r,c_{\sigma(r)}}(L_r)\Bigr)P_{n,i}=e_\alpha^{(n-1)}P_{n,i},$$ the sum in the middle running over the distinct orderings $\mathbf j$ of $c$. By step 4.1 the element $e_\alpha^{(n-1)}$ is a central idempotent of $kS_{n-1}$, and $P_{n,i}\in k[L_n]$ commutes with $kS_{n-1}$ by [F1]; hence $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$ is an idempotent commuting with $kS_{n-1}$. The idempotents $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$ are pairwise orthogonal because the sets $\{(\mathbf j,i):\mathbf j\in I_\alpha\}$ of sequences are disjoint for distinct pairs $(\alpha,i)$, and they sum to $1$ because every sequence of length $n$ has a unique last entry $i$ and a unique content $\alpha$ for its first $n-1$ entries. Consequently for every finite-dimensional $M$ the summands $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M$ are $kS_{n-1}$-submodules and $M=\bigoplus_{i,\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M$, which is $\operatorname{Res}M=\bigoplus_iE_iM$ in the notation of the statement.

*Induction side.* The same computation with $n$ replaced by $d+1$ shows that $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=e_\alpha^{(d)}P_{d+1,i}$ is an idempotent of $kS_{d+1}$ commuting with $kS_d$, that $\sum_{i,\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=1$ with pairwise orthogonal summands, and that $kS_{d+1}=\bigoplus_{i,\alpha}kS_{d+1}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$; hence for any finite-dimensional $M$, $$kS_{d+1}\otimes_{kS_d}M=\bigoplus_{i,\alpha}kS_{d+1}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}e_\alpha M=\bigoplus_iF_iM,$$ the middle step using $M=\bigoplus_\alpha e_\alpha M$ and the centrality of $e_\alpha$ in $kS_d$. This is $\operatorname{Ind}M=\bigoplus_iF_iM$.

*Exactness and duality.* Each $E_i$ is a direct sum of the functors $M\mapsto e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M$; a map $f:M\to N$ of $kS_n$-modules commutes with the action of the element $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$, so it restricts to a map $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M\to e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}N$, and each such functor is exact as a direct summand of the identity, hence additive and finite-dimensionality preserving. Each $F_i$ is a direct sum of the functors $M\mapsto kS_{d+1}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}e_\alpha M$, which are direct summands of induction $M\mapsto kS_{d+1}\otimes_{kS_d}M$; by [F5] $kS_{d+1}$ is free as a right $kS_d$-module, so induction, and with it each $F_i$, is exact, additive and finite-dimensionality preserving. For duality observe that $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$ is fixed by the antipode by step 1.2, and that the standard nondegenerate pairing $M\times M^*\to k$ satisfies $(xm,f)=(m,x^*f)$; hence for finite-dimensional $M$ the transpose of the projection on $M$ is the projection on $M^*$ and $(e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M)^*\cong e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M^*$, giving $E_i(M)^*\cong E_i(M^*)$. On the induction side the transpose identifies $(kS_{d+1}e\otimes_{kS_d}M)^*$ with $e\,kS_{d+1}\otimes_{kS_d}M^*$ through the antipode, and the antipode maps $e\,kS_{d+1}$ isomorphically to $kS_{d+1}e$ because $e$ is antipode-invariant; summing over $\alpha$ gives $F_i(M)^*\cong F_i(M^*)$. All identities are $k$-linear and natural, so they hold functorially in $M$.

*The block identification (recorded from the source).* The construction above proves that each $e_\alpha$ is a central idempotent and that distinct content sums are orthogonal. For a content vector that is the content of a partition of $n$, the source theorem (Kleshchev's survey, with the exact section and equation number recorded in the item's sources; proved from Lyle-Mathas, $\it{Blocks\ of\ cyclotomic\ Hecke\ algebras}$, Adv. Math. 216 (2007), and Brundan, $\it{Centers\ of\ degenerate\ cyclotomic\ Hecke\ algebras\ and\ parabolic\ category\ O}$, in the cyclotomic Hecke setting and specialized to the symmetric group case at $\xi=1$) identifies the corresponding nonzero $e_\alpha$ with a primitive central idempotent of $kS_n$, and conversely every primitive central idempotent of $kS_n$ is such an $e_\alpha$; by [F6] these are exactly the block idempotents. The primitivity and exhaustiveness assertions are the content of that cited block theorem and are not re-proved in this item; no later item of this page uses them, the definition and all uses of the functors $E_i,F_i$ resting on the centrality, idempotency, orthogonality and antipode-invariance proved in steps 1.1-7.1. For $n=0$ the empty sequence is the only index, $e(\varnothing)=1$ and $E_i$ is the zero functor on the zero module; the statements are vacuous and no case is excluded.

*An integral central identity.* In $\mathbb ZS_n$ one has $\prod_{r=1}^n(u+L_r)=\sum_{g\in S_n}u^{c(g)}g$, where $c(g)$ is the number of cycles, including fixed points. To prove this by induction, regard $S_{n-1}$ as fixing $n$. A term multiplied by $u$ leaves $n$ fixed and adds one cycle. A term multiplied by $(a,n)$ inserts $n$ in the cycle containing $a$, without changing its cycle count. Conversely, deleting a nonfixed $n$ from its cycle uniquely recovers the permutation in $S_{n-1}$ and the transposition used. Thus every permutation occurs exactly once. Comparing coefficients, each elementary symmetric polynomial $C_s$ in $L_1,\ldots,L_n$ is a sum of all permutations with $n-s$ cycles and hence is central; the identity and centrality remain true after reduction to $k$.

*Induction duality by a perfect coset pairing.* Put $G=S_{d+1}$, $H=S_d$, and let $\pi_H:kG\to kH$ retain the coefficients of the elements of $H$. For a finite-dimensional left $kH$-module $M$, with contragredient action $(a f)(m)=f(a^{-1}m)$, define $\langle g\otimes m,h\otimes f\rangle=f(\pi_H(h^{-1}g)m)$ between $\operatorname{Ind}M$ and $\operatorname{Ind}M^*$. For $a\in H$, the $kH$-bimodule property of $\pi_H$ gives $\pi_H(h^{-1}ga)=\pi_H(h^{-1}g)a$ and $\pi_H((ha)^{-1}g)=a^{-1}\pi_H(h^{-1}g)$; these identities prove balancing in the first and second tensor factors, respectively. Simultaneous left multiplication of $g,h$ by any element of $G$ leaves $h^{-1}g$ unchanged, proving $G$-invariance. On a finite left-coset transversal $T$ one has $\pi_H(s^{-1}r)=\delta_{s,r}1$ for $r,s\in T$. Thus the pairing is the direct sum of the perfect evaluations $M\times M^*\to k$ and is perfect by [F5]. For $e=e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$, right multiplication $R_e(g\otimes m)=ge\otimes m$ is a well-defined $G$-linear idempotent because $e$ commutes with $kH$. Let $\tau:kG\to k$ be the coefficient of $1$; directly on group elements, $\tau(xy)=\tau(yx)$. For every $b\in H$, the coefficient of $b$ in $ze$ equals $\tau(b^{-1}ze)=\tau(eb^{-1}z)=\tau(b^{-1}ez)$, since $e$ commutes with $b$. Therefore $\pi_H(ze)=\pi_H(ez)$ for all $z\in kG$. Writing $e^*$ for its antipode image, step 1.2 gives $e^*=e$, so expansion in the group basis yields $\langle R_e(g\otimes m),h\otimes f\rangle=f(\pi_H(h^{-1}ge)m)=f(\pi_H(eh^{-1}g)m)=\langle g\otimes m,R_e(h\otimes f)\rangle$. The two images of $R_e$ pair perfectly: a vector in either image annihilating the other annihilates the entire opposite space, since the opposite kernel is orthogonal to that image, and hence vanishes by perfectness. By tensor balancing, $ge\otimes m=ge\otimes e_\alpha m$, so these images are precisely $kG e\otimes_{kH}e_\alpha M$ and $kG e\otimes_{kH}e_\alpha M^*$. Distinct $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$ images are orthogonal by self-adjointness and projector orthogonality. Summing the perfect image pairings over $\alpha\in\mathcal C_d$ proves the natural $G$-isomorphism $F_i(M^*)\cong F_i(M)^*$; invariance supplies the contragredient action, and evaluation shows naturality in $M$. The construction uses finite transversals and holds over every characteristic, including $2$.

boundaries.evidence: A partition with no i-nodes has the empty word, which the definition already treats as reduced; the reduction and both selections are vacuous, so ε_i = φ_i = 0 and the definition assigns no good or cogood node.
Zeros are the cancelled positions of the word and the definition deletes them before the signs are read; residue 0 is an ordinary value of i, so a 0-node is treated like any other node.
A single i-node gives a one-letter reduced word (+ or −) and is selected as cogood or good accordingly; the definition also records that the survived signs have the shape + …… + − …… −.

The confluence argument recorded in the definition makes the reduced word and the outermost signs independent of the order of replacements, so the degenerate case of several possible cancellations has a unique outcome.
The good node is defined as the topmost surviving − and the cogood node as the bottommost surviving +; these endpoint selections and their uniqueness are part of the definition.
All lists are finite, ordered top to bottom, and the reduction is deterministic; no choice principle is used, as recorded in the definition statement.

Forward direction of the dictionary stated in the definition: a removable node that is normal in the c−r signature has a normal transpose in Brundan’s r−c convention, since the residue sign is reversed and transposed nodes reverse the order in their residue class, as recorded in the definition from Brundan’s transposed-node remark.

Reverse direction of the same dictionary: a removable node whose transpose is normal in Brundan’s convention is normal in the c−r signature, because transposition is an involution and the residue sign reversal is symmetric, so the two conventions match in both directions, as stated in the definition.

derivations.claim: $\Phi_M$ is a well-defined $kG$-linear map. For fixed $g,m$ the formula defines a function on $G$: if $xg\in H$ then $(xg)m\in M$, otherwise $0$. It is $k$-linear in $x$ by definition, and it is $kH$-linear: for $h\in H$ and $x\in G$, $\Phi_M(g\otimes m)(hx)=((hx)g)m$ if $hxg\in H$ and $0$ otherwise; since $hxg=(hx)g$ and $hxg\in H\iff xg\in H$ (as $h,h^{-1}\in H$), this equals $h((xg)m)=h\Phi_M(g\otimes m)(x)$ in the first case and $0$ in the second. Hence $\Phi_M(g\otimes m)\in\operatorname{Coind}_H^GM$. The map is $k$-linear and in the second tensor variable balanced: for $h\in H$, the functions $\Phi_M(gh\otimes m)$ and $\Phi_M(g\otimes hm)$ both send $x$ to $((xg)h)m=(xg)(hm)$ when $xg\in H$ and to $0$ otherwise; so $\Phi_M$ is well defined on the tensor product. Finally it is $kG$-linear: $\Phi_M(g_0g\otimes m)(x)=((xg_0)g)m$ if $xg_0g\in H$ and $0$ otherwise, and $(g_0\Phi_M(g\otimes m))(x)=\Phi_M(g\otimes m)(xg_0)=((xg_0)g)m$ if $xg_0g\in H$ and $0$ otherwise, the two conditions being the same.

The inverse on coinduced maps. Define, for $\varphi\in\operatorname{Coind}_H^GM$, $$\Psi_M(\varphi):=\sum_{t\in T}t^{-1}\otimes\varphi(t)\in kG\otimes_{kH}M.$$ The sum is finite because $T$ is finite by [F4]. The definition does not depend on the chosen transversal: if $T'$ is another and $t'\in T'$ lies in the left coset $tH$, say $t'=th$ with $h\in H$, then $t'^{-1}\otimes\varphi(t')=h^{-1}t^{-1}\otimes\varphi(th)=t^{-1}\otimes h^{-1}\varphi(th)=t^{-1}\otimes h^{-1}h\varphi(t)=t^{-1}\otimes\varphi(t)$, using the balancing relation of [F1] and the $kH$-linearity of $\varphi$. Hence $\Psi_M$ is a well-defined $k$-linear map $\operatorname{Coind}_H^GM\to\operatorname{Ind}_H^GM$.

$\Phi_M\Psi_M=\mathrm{id}$. Let $\varphi\in\operatorname{Coind}_H^GM$ and $x\in G$. By [F4] let $t_0\in T$ and $h_0\in H$ be the unique elements with $x=h_0t_0$, so that $x\in Ht_0$. Then $\Phi_M(\Psi_M(\varphi))(x)=\sum_{t\in T}\Phi_M(t^{-1}\otimes\varphi(t))(x)=\sum_{t\in T,\ xt^{-1}\in H}(xt^{-1})\varphi(t)$. Since $xt^{-1}\in H\iff x\in Ht\iff Ht_0=Ht\iff t=t_0$, exactly one term survives, and it equals $(h_0t_0t_0^{-1})\varphi(t_0)=h_0\varphi(t_0)=\varphi(h_0t_0)=\varphi(x)$, using $kH$-linearity of $\varphi$.

$\Psi_M\Phi_M=\mathrm{id}$. Let $g\in G$ and $m\in M$. Then $\Psi_M(\Phi_M(g\otimes m))=\sum_{t\in T}t^{-1}\otimes\Phi_M(g\otimes m)(t)=\sum_{t\in T,\ tg\in H}t^{-1}\otimes(tg)m$. The elements $t$ with $tg\in H$ are those with $t\in Hg^{-1}$, which is a single left coset of $H$; by [F4] the transversal $T$ meets it in exactly one element $t_0$, so the sum has one term $t_0^{-1}\otimes(t_0g)m$. Writing $h:=(t_0g)^{-1}\in H$ and using the balancing relation, $t_0^{-1}\otimes(t_0g)m=(gh)\otimes(t_0g)m=g\otimes h(t_0g)m=g\otimes m$. Since the elements $g\otimes m$ span $\operatorname{Ind}_H^GM$ over $k$, $\Psi_M\Phi_M$ is the identity.

Naturality and consequences. If $f:M\to M'$ is a $kH$-map, then for all $g,m,x$ one has $\Phi_{M'}(g\otimes f(m))(x)=f(\Phi_M(g\otimes m)(x))$, because the formula is evaluated by multiplication in $M$ or $M'$ and $f$ is linear; hence $\Phi$ is a natural transformation, and by steps 2.1 and 2.2 each $\Phi_M$ is an isomorphism with natural inverse $\Psi_M$. Therefore $\operatorname{Ind}_H^G\cong\operatorname{Coind}_H^G$ as functors, and [F2] yields that induction is both a left and a right adjoint of restriction: the left adjunction is its induction adjunction, and the right adjunction is transported across this natural isomorphism from the coinduction adjunction. Induction $-\otimes_{kH}kG$ is right exact, and coinduction $\operatorname{Hom}_{kH}(kG,-)$ is left exact; a natural isomorphism between the two functors therefore makes induction exact, in agreement with the freeness of $kG$ over $kH$ recorded in [F3]. No hypothesis on $k$, on characteristic, or on splitting is used, and the only selection made is the finite transversal $T$ of least representatives.

citations.quote:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ and let $L_1,\dots,L_n\in kS_n$
be the Jucys-Murphy elements $L_r=\sum_{s<r}(s,r)$ of the symmetric group
algebra ([[def-jucys-murphy-elements-of-the-symmetric-group-algebra]]). Recall
that they commute pairwise
([[cor-jucys-murphy-elements-commute-pairwise]]), and for $r\le n$ the
element $L_r$ lies in the subalgebra $kS_r\subseteq kS_n$ and therefore
commutes with $S_{r-1}$.

**(i) Primary idempotents.** In the commutative subalgebra
$k[L_1,\dots,L_n]\subseteq kS_n$ the minimal polynomial of each $L_r$ on the
regular module splits into linear factors $X-a$ with $a$ in the prime field
$\mathbb F_p\subseteq k$, and the commuting family admits the following
simultaneous primary decomposition. There are pairwise orthogonal idempotents
$P_{r,a}\in k[L_r]\subseteq k[L_1,\dots,L_n]$, indexed by $r\in\{1,\dots,n\}$
and $a\in\mathbb F_p$, with
$$\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_p}P_{r,a}=1,\qquad P_{r,a}P_{r,b}=\delta_{a,b}P_{r,a},$$
such that for every finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module $M$ the action of
$P_{r,a}$ on $M$ is the projection onto the generalized eigenspace
$M_{r,a}=\{m\in M:(L_r-a)^Nm=0\text{ for }N\gg0\}$. The $P_{r,a}$ for
different $r$ commute, and for each sequence $\mathbf i=(i_1,\dots,i_n)$
with entries in $\mathbb F_p$ the products
$$e(\mathbf i):=\prod_{r=1}^nP_{r,i_r}\ \in\ k[L_1,\dots,L_n]$$
are pairwise orthogonal idempotents with $\sum_{\mathbf i}e(\mathbf i)=1$ and
$e(\mathbf i)M=M_{\mathbf i}$, the simultaneous generalized weight space
$M_{\mathbf i}=\{m:(L_r-i_r)^Nm=0\ \forall r,\ N\gg0\}$. Every $P_{r,a}$ and
every $e(\mathbf i)$ is fixed by the antipode $g\mapsto g^{-1}$ of $kS_n$.

**(ii) Content sums and blocks.** The symmetric group $S_n$ permutes the
coordinates of sequences, and two sequences are called *equivalent* when they
differ by a permutation, i.e. when they have the same content (the same
multiset of entries of $\mathbb F_p$). Write $\mathcal C_n=(\mathbb F_p)^n/S_n$ for the set of content classes
(equivalently, multisets of $n$ residues). For $\alpha\in\mathcal C_n$ let
$I_\alpha$ be the set of sequences representing $\alpha$, and put
$$e_\alpha:=\sum_{\mathbf i\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf i)\ \in\ kS_n .$$
Each $e_\alpha$ is a central idempotent of $kS_n$, and distinct $e_\alpha$
are orthogonal; the nonzero $e_\alpha$ are exactly the primitive central
idempotents, that is the block idempotents of $kS_n$
([[def-p-blocks-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]), and every block
idempotent of $kS_n$ is of the form $e_\alpha$: this last identification of
the content sums with the blocks is the block theorem of Lyle-Mathas and
Brundan recorded as (2.41) in Kleshchev's survey (printed p. 11), with the
content of the block being the content of any of its partitions. The present
item proves the centrality, idempotency and orthogonality of the sums
$e_\alpha$ and then uses only those properties; primitivity and
exhaustiveness are recorded from the cited block theorem, not re-proved here.

**(iii) Residue-summand functors.** For a finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module
$M$, a residue $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and a content class
$\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}$, put
$$e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}:=\sum_{\mathbf j\in I_\alpha}e((\mathbf j,i)) \ =\ e_\alpha^{(n-1)}\,P_{n,i},$$
where $(\mathbf j,i)$ denotes concatenation, $e_\alpha^{(n-1)}=\sum_{\mathbf
j\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf j)$ is the content sum computed in $kS_{n-1}$ and
regarded in $kS_n$ through the inclusion $kS_{n-1}\subseteq kS_n$, and
$P_{n,i}\in k[L_n]$. Each $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$ is an idempotent of $kS_n$
commuting with $kS_{n-1}$, the family
$\{e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\}_{i\in\mathbb F_p,\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}}$ is a family of pairwise orthogonal
idempotents with $\sum_{i,\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=1$, and
$$E_iM:=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M =\bigoplus_{\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M$$
is a $kS_{n-1}$-submodule of the restricted module with
$$\operatorname{Res}^{S_n}_{S_{n-1}}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}E_iM .$$
Dually, for a finite-dimensional $kS_d$-module $M$ of content
$\alpha\in\mathcal C_d$, i.e. $M=e_\alpha^{(d)}M$, put
$$F_iM:=kS_{d+1}\,e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}M \qquad(i\in\mathbb Z/p),$$
with $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=e_\alpha^{(d)}P_{d+1,i}\in kS_{d+1}$; for a
general finite-dimensional $M$, with the sum indexed by $\alpha\in\mathcal C_d$, put
$F_iM:=\bigoplus_\alpha kS_{d+1}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}e_\alpha M$.
Then $\operatorname{Ind}^{S_{d+1}}_{S_d}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}F_iM$,
and all the functors $E_i,F_i$ are additive and exact, preserve
finite-dimensionality, and commute with contragredient duality, because the
projectors are fixed by the antipode. All statements hold at $p=2$; the
construction is choice-free.

Let $p>0$ and let $\mu$ be a $p$-restricted partition, so that
$\mu_i-\mu_{i+1}<p$ for all $i\ge1$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A node $(r,c)$ of
the Young diagram $[\mu]$ is an **$i$-node** if its residue
$$\operatorname{res}(r,c):=c-r\bmod p$$
equals $i\in\mathbb Z/p$; the $i$-nodes of $\mu$ are its addable and removable
nodes of residue $i$
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]).

**The reduced $i$-signature.** Fix $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and list the $i$-nodes
of $\mu$ as $A_1,\dots,A_n$ from top to bottom, that is, in increasing row
index and, for equal row index, in increasing column index. Form the word
$\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m=+$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m=-$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r<s$, $\sigma_r=-$,
$\sigma_s=+$ and $\sigma_{r+1}=\dots=\sigma_{s-1}=0$, replace $\sigma_r$ and
$\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$. The
resulting **reduced $i$-signature** has the form $+\cdots+- \cdots-$ with the
zeros deleted, and the nodes attached to its signs are:

- the **normal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the removable nodes corresponding to
  the $-$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **good $i$-node** is the topmost (first listed) of the normal $i$-nodes;
- the **conormal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the addable nodes corresponding to
  the $+$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **cogood $i$-node** is the bottommost (last listed) of the conormal
  $i$-nodes.

Write $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ and $\varphi_i(\mu)$ for the numbers of normal and
of conormal $i$-nodes of $\mu$; the good $i$-node exists exactly when
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, and the cogood $i$-node exactly when
$\varphi_i(\mu)>0$. At most one good and at most one cogood $i$-node occur,
for each residue.

**Well-definedness.** Each reduction step deletes two nonzero entries, so any
sequence of steps terminates after at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ steps, and in
the resulting word no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$: otherwise, take two
nonzero entries that are consecutive among the nonzero entries of the current
word and are ordered $-$, $+$; all entries strictly between them are $0$ by
the choice, so the pair would still be reducible. Hence, after deleting the zero entries, a terminal word is
$+^a-^b$ for some $a,b\ge0$; cancelled positions remain in their original
places and need not form a contiguous block. The terminal word does not depend on the
order in which reducible pairs are chosen: two reducible pairs cannot overlap
partially, because an endpoint of one pair lying strictly inside the other
would be a nonzero entry in a position that the other pair requires to be
$0$, and pairs sharing exactly one endpoint would similarly place a nonzero
entry strictly inside the other pair; so any two reducible pairs are either
disjoint (and the corresponding steps commute) or equal, there are no
critical pairs, and the rewriting relation is locally confluent. Uniqueness follows
by induction on the number of nonzero entries. A terminal word admits no
step. Otherwise, two distinct first steps commute and reach a common word
after one further step each. All these successor words have fewer nonzero
entries, so the induction hypothesis identifies their terminal words. Thus
any two reduction sequences have the same terminal word; in it the first surviving $-$ and the last surviving
$+$ are unique positions whenever they exist. Thus the reduced signature,
the sets of normal and conormal nodes, and the good and cogood nodes are well
defined. The empty partition has the unique addable node $(1,1)$, of residue $0$,
and no removable nodes. Its $0$-signature is $(+)$ and its other signatures
are empty. Thus $\varepsilon_i(\varnothing)=0$ for every $i$,
$\varphi_0(\varnothing)=1$, and $\varphi_i(\varnothing)=0$ for $i\ne0$.
It has no good node and its cogood $0$-node is $(1,1)$.

**Convention warning.** The residue $c-r$ used here is the negative of
Brundan's $\ell$-residue $r-c$, and a removable node of $\mu$ is normal here
exactly when its transposed node is normal in Brundan's sense for the
transpose partition $\mu'$; lists of addable and removable nodes, and the
signs of the residues, must never be silently mixed between the two
conventions
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting
$p$-modular system for $S_n$, so that $k$ is a splitting field of
characteristic $p$ for $S_n$ and all its subgroups
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). For a partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ let
$$S^\lambda_k=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z},\qquad R^\lambda=S^\lambda_k\cap(S^\lambda_k)^{\perp},\qquad D^\lambda=S^\lambda_k/R^\lambda$$
be the modular Specht quotient of
[[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]], defined using the reduced
integral tabloid form on $M^\lambda_k$.

1. **Simple heads.** If $\lambda$ is $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda\ne0$ is
   self-dual and absolutely irreducible, and it is the simple head of
   $S^\lambda_k$, whose unique maximal submodule is
   $R^\lambda=\operatorname{rad}(S^\lambda_k)$. If $\lambda$ is not
   $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda=0$.
2. **Pairwise inequivalent.** If $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ are both $p$-regular
   and $D^\lambda\cong D^\mu$ as $k[S_n]$-modules, then $\lambda=\mu$.
3. **Complete set.** Every simple $k[S_n]$-module is isomorphic to $D^\lambda$
   for exactly one $p$-regular partition $\lambda\vdash n$. Equivalently, as
   $\lambda$ ranges over the $p$-regular partitions of $n$, the modules
   $D^\lambda$ form a complete set of representatives of the isomorphism
   classes of simple $k[S_n]$-modules; in particular the number of simple
   $k[S_n]$-modules equals the number of $p$-regular partitions of $n$.

No absolutely irreducible module outside the family $\{D^\lambda\}$ is
constructed, and the statement asserts nothing about fields that are not
splitting fields for $S_n$. The proof uses no averaging and no division by a
group order, and the case $n=0$ and characteristic $2$ are included.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting
$p$-modular system for $S_n$, so that $k$ is a splitting field of
characteristic $p$ for $S_n$
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). For $\mu\vdash n$
write $S^\mu_k=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\mu_{\mathbb Z}$ for the field-valued
Specht module, $D^\mu=S^\mu_k/R^\mu$ for its modular form quotient
([[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]]), and let
$$S(\mu):=(S^\mu_k)^*=\operatorname{Hom}_k(S^\mu_k,k),\qquad (\sigma\cdot f)(x):=f(\sigma^{-1}x)$$
be the **dual Specht module**, with
$$D(\mu):=\operatorname{hd}\bigl(S(\mu)\bigr) =S(\mu)/\operatorname{rad}\bigl(S(\mu)\bigr)$$
its head ([[def-module-radical-socle-head-and-loewy-series]]). Let
$\mu'$ be the conjugate partition, and let
$S^{\mu'}_k\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ be the tensor product of
$k[S_n]$-modules with the diagonal action
$\sigma\cdot(x\otimes w)=(\sigma\cdot x)\otimes(\sigma\cdot w)$, where
$\operatorname{sgn}$ is the one-dimensional sign representation
([[def-sign-representation-and-restriction-of-a-representation]],
[[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]).

1. **Dual Specht versus sign-twisted conjugate.** If $\mu$ is $p$-restricted
   (equivalently, by
   [[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]], $\mu'$ is $p$-regular),
   then $S(\mu)\cong S^{\mu'}_k\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$; consequently
   $S(\mu)$ is nonzero with simple head
   $$D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn},$$
   a nonzero simple $k[S_n]$-module that is self-dual and absolutely
   irreducible.
2. **Equivalent form for $p$-regular labels.** If $\lambda\vdash n$ is
   $p$-regular, then $\lambda'$ is $p$-restricted and
   $$D^\lambda\cong D(\lambda')\otimes\operatorname{sgn}.$$
3. **The two labellings.** The map $\mu\mapsto D(\mu)$ is a bijection from
   the set of $p$-restricted partitions of $n$ to the set of isomorphism
   classes of simple $k[S_n]$-modules; that is, every simple
   $k[S_n]$-module is isomorphic to $D(\mu)$ for exactly one $p$-restricted
   $\mu\vdash n$.

In characteristic $2$ the sign representation is the trivial representation,
so the formulas read $D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}$ and $D^\lambda\cong D(\lambda')$;
the transposition is still required, and the two labellings coincide only
for self-conjugate partitions. No step divides by a group order or uses
averaging, and $n=0$ is included.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $F$ be a
field of characteristic $p$. Let $\beta_F$ be the reduced integral tabloid
form on $M^\lambda_F=F\otimes_{\mathbb Z}M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$, with
orthonormal tabloid basis, and let
$$S^\lambda_F\subseteq M^\lambda_F,\qquad R^\lambda_F:=S^\lambda_F\cap(S^\lambda_F)^{\perp},\qquad D^\lambda_F:=S^\lambda_F/R^\lambda_F,$$
where $V^{\perp}=\{x\in M^\lambda_F:\beta_F(x,v)=0\text{ for all }v\in V\}$
([[def-integral-tabloid-bilinear-form-and-specht-gram-matrix]],
[[thm-james-submodule-theorem-over-an-arbitrary-field]]). Let $G_\lambda$ be
the Gram matrix of the integral tabloid form in the standard-polytabloid
basis of the integral Specht lattice $S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$, and let
$g_\lambda$ be the positive greatest common divisor of its entries
([[def-integral-specht-lattice-and-base-change]],
[[lem-specht-gram-gcd-detects-p-regularity]]). Write $G_\lambda\bmod p$ for
the entrywise image of $G_\lambda$ in $F$, a matrix with entries in $F$.
Then:

1. **Vanishing criterion.**
   $$D^\lambda_F=0\iff p\mid G_{ij}\text{ for all }i,j \iff p\mid g_\lambda\iff\lambda\text{ is not }p\text{-regular},$$
   and equivalently $D^\lambda_F\ne0$ if and only if $z_j(\lambda)<p$ for
   every $j\ge1$, where $z_j(\lambda)$ is the number of parts of $\lambda$
   equal to $j$.
2. **Dimension.** $\dim_FD^\lambda_F=\operatorname{rank}_F(G_\lambda\bmod p)$;
   this dimension is determined by $\lambda$ and $p$ alone, and it is
   positive exactly when $\lambda$ is $p$-regular.
3. **Structure when nonzero.** If $\lambda$ is $p$-regular, then
   $D^\lambda_F\ne0$ is the simple, self-dual and absolutely irreducible
   head of $S^\lambda_F$, and $R^\lambda_F$ is the unique maximal submodule
   of $S^\lambda_F$, equal to the module radical
   $\operatorname{rad}(S^\lambda_F)$.

For the $k$ of a splitting $p$-modular system $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ for $S_n$,
$D^\lambda_k$ is the modular Specht quotient $D^\lambda$ of
[[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]], so the criterion above
decides for which $\lambda$ that quotient vanishes. No simplicity of
$S^\lambda_F$ itself is asserted.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra and $M$ a finite-dimensional left
$A$-module.

- Its **radical** is
  $$   \operatorname{rad}(M)=J(A)M,   $$
  equivalently the intersection of the maximal submodules, by
  [[thm-module-radical-is-jacobson-radical-times-the-module]].

- Its **socle** $\operatorname{Soc}(M)$ is the sum of all simple submodules, as
  in [[def-socle-of-a-module]].

- Its **head** or **top** is the quotient
  $$   \operatorname{hd}(M):=M/\operatorname{rad}(M),   $$
  formed using [[def-quotient-module]].

- Its **Loewy series** is the descending radical filtration
  $$   M\supseteq \operatorname{rad}(M)\supseteq \operatorname{rad}^2(M)\supseteq\cdots   $$
  together with the corresponding semisimple layers
  $\operatorname{rad}^i(M)/\operatorname{rad}^{i+1}(M)$.

The simple subquotients appearing in the Loewy layers are simple in the sense
of [[def-simple-module]].

boundaries.evidence: At d = 1, μ = (1) the right-hand side is the single term D(∅) = k, the empty partition being a legitimate label, and the restriction to the trivial group is k (step 4.1); the empty sum occurs exactly for a residue with ε_i = 0 (step 1.2).
The case ε_i(μ) = 0 is where the summand vanishes: step 1.2 sets soc(E_iD(μ)) = 0 then and the displayed sum omits that residue.
d = 1 is worked in step 4.1: the display has the single term D(∅) and soc(D(μ)↓_{S_0}) = k = D(∅).
p = 2 is allowed: step 1.1 decomposes over i ∈ Z/2 and step 1.2 invokes the recorded theorem, applied in every positive characteristic in the statement.
No residue class is special: steps 1.2 and 2.1 sum over all i ∈ Z/p and step 3.1 compares any pair i ≠ j.
The residues and good nodes are finite in number and canonically determined by the definition; no choice principle is used.

The only biconditional appearing in the item is the completely reducible special case quoted in the statement as a separate source theorem of Kleshchev II; the forward direction (semisimple restriction implies every normal node is good) is explicitly not asserted here, the corollary proving the equality of the socle with the good-node sum in steps 1.1 to 4.1.

The converse direction (every normal node good implies semisimplicity) is part of the same quoted source statement and is deliberately excluded from the claims of this corollary; no step of the proof uses or proves it.

derivations.claim: By [F1] the restriction decomposes as $\operatorname{Res}D(\mu)=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}E_iD(\mu)$ with each $E_iD(\mu)$ a $kS_{d-1}$-submodule, and by [F5] the socle of the restriction is the direct sum $\bigoplus_i\operatorname{soc}(E_iD(\mu))$.

By the recorded socle theorem [F3], for each residue $i$ the module $\operatorname{soc}(E_iD(\mu))$ is $D(\mu\setminus A_i)$ when $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$ and is $0$ when $\varepsilon_i(\mu)=0$; by [F3] each $\mu\setminus A_i$ is a $p$-restricted partition of $d-1$, so each displayed $D(\mu\setminus A_i)$ is a simple $kS_{d-1}$-module in the sense of [F4].

Summing the descriptions of step 1.2 over the finitely many residues $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and using step 1.1 gives $$\operatorname{soc}_{S_{d-1}}\bigl(D(\mu){\downarrow}_{S_{d-1}}\bigr)=\bigoplus_{i:\,\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0}D(\mu\setminus A_i).$$

The sum is multiplicity-free and its summands are pairwise non-isomorphic: if $i\ne j$ and both $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ and $\varepsilon_j(\mu)$ are positive, then the good nodes $A_i$ and $A_j$ have different residues and are therefore distinct nodes of $\mu$, so the $p$-restricted partitions $\mu\setminus A_i$ and $\mu\setminus A_j$ of $d-1$ are distinct by [F2]; by [F4] their simple modules $D(\mu\setminus A_i)$ and $D(\mu\setminus A_j)$ are non-isomorphic. Each residue contributes its summand once, so each isomorphism class occurs with multiplicity one in the displayed socle.

The displayed decomposition of step 2.1 has the left-hand side $\operatorname{soc}_{S_{d-1}}(D(\mu)\downarrow_{S_{d-1}})$ and, by step 3.1, is a multiplicity-free sum over distinct simple modules with one summand per residue $i$ satisfying $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$. No claim is made here about the restriction being semisimple. In the smallest case $d=1$ one has $\mu=(1)$, and the only node of residue $0$ is the removable node $(1,1)$, so $\varepsilon_0(\mu)=1$ and the right-hand side is the single term $D(\varnothing)=k$, while the restriction to the trivial group $S_0$ is $k$ itself, in agreement with the display; this is the smallest instance in which the summands carry the empty partition as a label.

$+$ are unique positions whenever they exist. Thus the reduced signature,
the sets of normal and conormal nodes, and the good and cogood nodes are well
defined. The empty partition has the unique addable node $(1,1)$, of residue $0$,
and no removable nodes. Its $0$-signature is $(+)$ and its other signatures
are empty. Thus $\varepsilon_i(\varnothing)=0$ for every $i$,
$\varphi_0(\varnothing)=1$, and $\varphi_i(\varnothing)=0$ for $i\ne0$.
It has no good node and its cogood $0$-node is $(1,1)$.

**Convention warning.** The residue $c-r$ used here is the negative of
Brundan's $\ell$-residue $r-c$, and a removable node of $\mu$ is normal here
exactly when its transposed node is normal in Brundan's sense for the
transpose partition $\mu'$; lists of addable and removable nodes, and the
signs of the residues, must never be silently mixed between the two
conventions
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ with Young diagram $[\lambda]$, and let
$\mu\vdash n-1$ and $\nu\vdash n+1$ denote partitions of the neighbouring
sizes ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

A node $x\in[\lambda]$ is **removable** if deleting it leaves a Young diagram,
that is, if there is a partition $\mu\vdash n-1$ with
$$[\mu]=[\lambda]\setminus\{x\};$$
such a $\mu$ is unique because a partition is determined by its diagram. A
point $y\notin[\lambda]$ is **addable** for $\lambda$ if inserting it leaves a
Young diagram, that is, if there is a partition $\nu\vdash n+1$ with
$$[\nu]=[\lambda]\cup\{y\};$$
again $\nu$ is unique. We write $\operatorname{Rem}(\lambda)$ and
$\operatorname{Add}(\lambda)$ for the sets of removable and of addable nodes
of $\lambda$.

Since $[\lambda]=\{(i,j):1\le i\le k,\ 1\le j\le\lambda_i\}$ is determined by
the inequalities $1\le j\le\lambda_i$, the two conditions have the following
row form. Write $\lambda_{k+1}:=0$ for a partition $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$.
A node $(i,\lambda_i)$ is removable if and only if
$\lambda_i>\lambda_{i+1}$: deleting the last node of row $i$ keeps the row
lengths weakly decreasing exactly when row $i+1$ is strictly shorter, and no
node $(i,j)$ with $j<\lambda_i$ can be deleted, since the node
$(i,j+1)$ would then have no node to its left. Similarly a node
$(i,\lambda_i+1)$ with $1\le i\le k$ is addable if and only if $i=1$ or
$\lambda_{i-1}>\lambda_i$, the node $(k+1,1)$ opening a new row is always
addable, and these are all the addable nodes. In particular a row endpoint of
$[\lambda]$ is removable only if no node of $[\lambda]$ lies immediately
below it.

For the empty partition the diagram is empty, so
$\operatorname{Rem}(\varnothing)=\emptyset$, while
$\operatorname{Add}(\varnothing)=\{(1,1)\}$ is a single node, whose insertion
produces the partition $(1)$.

Let $p$ be a prime and let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition of $n\ge0$ with
parts $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_k\ge1$ and conjugate partition
$\lambda'$, whose $j$-th part is the number $\lambda'_j=\#\{i:\lambda_i\ge j\}$
of nodes of $[\lambda]$ in column $j$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). For $j\ge1$ let
$$z_j(\lambda):=\#\{\,i:\lambda_i=j\,\}$$
be the multiplicity with which the positive integer $j$ occurs as a part of
$\lambda$; only finitely many $z_j$ are nonzero.

- $\lambda$ is **$p$-regular** when every positive part of $\lambda$ occurs
  fewer than $p$ times, that is, when $z_j(\lambda)<p$ for every $j\ge1$.
- $\lambda$ is **$p$-restricted** when $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<p$ for every
  $i\ge1$, where the sequence is padded by the trailing zeros
  $\lambda_i:=0$ for $i>k$.

Both conditions are finite families of inequalities. For $i>k$ one has
$\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}=0<p$, so the restrictedness condition is the finite
list for $1\le i\le k$. The empty partition $\varnothing\vdash0$ has no parts
and $k=0$, so $z_j(\varnothing)=0<p$ and $0-0=0<p$ for every $j,i\ge1$: it is
simultaneously $p$-regular and $p$-restricted for every prime $p$.

The two conditions are exchanged by conjugation: **$\lambda$ is $p$-restricted
if and only if $\lambda'$ is $p$-regular.** The number of columns of $[\lambda]$
of height exactly $i$ is the difference $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}$ of consecutive
parts, and these heights are precisely the parts of $\lambda'$, so the
multiplicity of the part $i$ in $\lambda'$ is $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}$; the
stated equivalence compares the same integers with $p$.

The names record two genuinely different label conventions used later on this
page: James's modular simple modules $D^\lambda$ are labelled by **$p$-regular**
$\lambda$. Dual Specht modules themselves are defined for every partition;
their simple heads give the **$p$-restricted** labelling of simple modules,
related to the first convention by transposition and a sign twist. Neither
class of partitions contains the other in general.

Let $p>0$ and let $\mu$ be a $p$-restricted partition, so that
$\mu_i-\mu_{i+1}<p$ for all $i\ge1$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A node $(r,c)$ of
the Young diagram $[\mu]$ is an **$i$-node** if its residue
$$\operatorname{res}(r,c):=c-r\bmod p$$
equals $i\in\mathbb Z/p$; the $i$-nodes of $\mu$ are its addable and removable
nodes of residue $i$
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]).

**The reduced $i$-signature.** Fix $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and list the $i$-nodes
of $\mu$ as $A_1,\dots,A_n$ from top to bottom, that is, in increasing row
index and, for equal row index, in increasing column index. Form the word
$\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m=+$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m=-$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r<s$, $\sigma_r=-$,
$\sigma_s=+$ and $\sigma_{r+1}=\dots=\sigma_{s-1}=0$, replace $\sigma_r$ and
$\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$. The
resulting **reduced $i$-signature** has the form $+\cdots+- \cdots-$ with the
zeros deleted, and the nodes attached to its signs are:

- the **normal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the removable nodes corresponding to
  the $-$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **good $i$-node** is the topmost (first listed) of the normal $i$-nodes;
- the **conormal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the addable nodes corresponding to
  the $+$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **cogood $i$-node** is the bottommost (last listed) of the conormal
  $i$-nodes.

Write $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ and $\varphi_i(\mu)$ for the numbers of normal and
of conormal $i$-nodes of $\mu$; the good $i$-node exists exactly when
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, and the cogood $i$-node exactly when
$\varphi_i(\mu)>0$. At most one good and at most one cogood $i$-node occur,
for each residue.

**Well-definedness.** Each reduction step deletes two nonzero entries, so any
sequence of steps terminates after at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ steps, and in
the resulting word no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$: otherwise, take two
nonzero entries that are consecutive among the nonzero entries of the current
word and are ordered $-$, $+$; all entries strictly between them are $0$ by
the choice, so the pair would still be reducible. Hence, after deleting the zero entries, a terminal word is
$+^a-^b$ for some $a,b\ge0$; cancelled positions remain in their original
places and need not form a contiguous block. The terminal word does not depend on the
order in which reducible pairs are chosen: two reducible pairs cannot overlap
partially, because an endpoint of one pair lying strictly inside the other
would be a nonzero entry in a position that the other pair requires to be
$0$, and pairs sharing exactly one endpoint would similarly place a nonzero
entry strictly inside the other pair; so any two reducible pairs are either
disjoint (and the corresponding steps commute) or equal, there are no
critical pairs, and the rewriting relation is locally confluent. Uniqueness follows
by induction on the number of nonzero entries. A terminal word admits no
step. Otherwise, two distinct first steps commute and reach a common word
after one further step each. All these successor words have fewer nonzero
entries, so the induction hypothesis identifies their terminal words. Thus
any two reduction sequences have the same terminal word; in it the first surviving $-$ and the last surviving
$+$ are unique positions whenever they exist. Thus the reduced signature,
the sets of normal and conormal nodes, and the good and cogood nodes are well
defined. The empty partition has the unique addable node $(1,1)$, of residue $0$,
and no removable nodes. Its $0$-signature is $(+)$ and its other signatures
are empty. Thus $\varepsilon_i(\varnothing)=0$ for every $i$,
$\varphi_0(\varnothing)=1$, and $\varphi_i(\varnothing)=0$ for $i\ne0$.
It has no good node and its cogood $0$-node is $(1,1)$.

**Convention warning.** The residue $c-r$ used here is the negative of
Brundan's $\ell$-residue $r-c$, and a removable node of $\mu$ is normal here
exactly when its transposed node is normal in Brundan's sense for the
transpose partition $\mu'$; lists of addable and removable nodes, and the
signs of the residues, must never be silently mixed between the two
conventions
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

boundaries.evidence: For the empty partition the only 0-node is the addable node (1,1), so f̃_0∅ = (1) while ẽ_i∅ is undefined for every i; this is the base case used in steps 5.1 and 6.1.
Residue 0 is ordinary: the empty partition has a cogood addition in residue 0 and the operators are defined for i = 0 like any other residue (step 6.1).
Rank 1 is covered by steps 3.1 and 4.1: deleting the single removable node and adding the single cogood node are inverse moves, and step 5.1 states the inverse property for all ranks.
p = 2 is included: step 3.2 uses only the inequality μ_{r−1} − μ_r ≤ p − 1 and step 3.3 the analogous one, so both restrictedness proofs apply verbatim at p = 2, where differences are at most 1.
The endpoint selections are exactly step 2.1: the first surviving − and the last surviving + are compared there, and steps 3.1 and 4.1 transfer the comparison to partitions.
The operators are defined by deterministic finite selections from the reduced word; no choice principle is used, as recorded in step 6.1.
Forward: if ν = ẽ_iμ then the good node A of μ is cogood in ν and f̃_iν = ν ∪ A = μ, proved in step 5.1 from step 3.1.
Reverse: if μ = f̃_iν then the cogood node B of ν is good in μ and ẽ_iμ = μ ∖ B = ν, proved in step 5.1 from step 4.1.

derivations.claim: *The stack algorithm computes the normal form.* The stack algorithm of [F3] terminates with a word containing no $-$ before a $+$ (a surviving $-$ stays on the stack and blocks the stack from being empty, so no later $+$ survives after it), and the reduction relation is confluent by [F3], so the surviving signs read in order are the reduced signature with zero entries deleted, $+^a-^b$; in particular the good node corresponds to the first surviving $-$ and the cogood node to the last surviving $+$.

*Comparison of the $i$-words.* Let $\mu$ be a partition and $X$ a removable $i$-node of $\mu$; put $
u:=\mu\setminus X$. By [F2] the $i$-nodes of $
u$ are obtained from those of $\mu$ by removing $X$ from the removable list and inserting $X$ into the addable list, all other $i$-nodes and their top-to-bottom order being unchanged; hence the $i$-signature words of $\mu$ and $
u$ have the same length and the same entries except at the position $p$ of $X$, where the word of $\mu$ has $-$ and the word of $
u$ has $+$.

*First surviving $-$ versus last surviving $+$.* Let $w$ be a signature word with $w_p=-$, let $w'$ be $w$ with the entry at $p$ changed to $+$, let $u$ be the prefix of $w$ strictly before $p$, and let $s$ be the suffix strictly after $p$. We prove that $p$ is the position of the first surviving $-$ of $w$ if and only if $p$ is the position of the last surviving $+$ of $w'$. Let $S$ be the stack of [F3] after scanning $u$; the prefix of $w'$ before $p$ is the same word $u$, so the same stack $S$ is present there. If $S$ is nonempty, let $q$ be its bottom entry; scanning $w$ further, $q$ can leave the stack only by being cancelled by a $+$ that has first cancelled every entry above it, in particular the entry at $p$, so either $q$ survives, giving a surviving $-$ before $p$, or the entry $p$ is cancelled before $q$ and does not survive; in both cases $p$ is not the first surviving $-$ of $w$. Similarly, scanning $w'$ the entry at $p$ is a $+$, which survives only if the stack just before it is empty, so if $S$ is nonempty then $p$ does not survive and is not the last surviving $+$ of $w'$. Hence both events force $S$ to be empty, and we may assume this. With $S$ empty, push the $-$ at $p$ in the scan of $w$; while this entry is alive, the pending entries above it after scanning a prefix $q$ of $s$ are the $-$ signs of $q$ not yet cancelled, and since no $+$ has yet occurred at height $0$, that number is $\#-(q)-\#+(q)$. Consequently $p$ is cancelled at the first $+$ of $s$ whose preceding prefix $q$ has $\#+(q)=\#-(q)$, and such a $+$ exists if and only if some prefix $q$ of $s$ has $\#+(q)>\#-(q)$: counts change by one at each symbol, so a strict surplus arises only across a step of equality, and conversely a prefix with equality followed by a $+$ would create a strict surplus. Thus, with $S$ empty, the entry at $p$ survives in $w$ if and only if $$(C)\quad \#+(q)\le\#-(q)\quad\text{for every prefix }q\text{ of }s.$$ In $w'$, the $+$ at $p$ arrives at the empty stack $S$ and survives; after it, a later $+$ of $s$ survives exactly when the stack is empty at its arrival. If (C) holds and a $+$ of $s$ survived, with preceding prefix $q$, then all $-$ of $q$ were cancelled, so $\#-(q)\le\#+(q)$, while (C) applied to the prefix $q$ extended by that $+$ gives $\#+(q)+1\le\#-(q)$, a contradiction; hence no later $+$ survives. Conversely, if (C) fails then some $+$ of $s$ survives: the stack height after a prefix $q$ of $s$ equals $\#-(q)-\#+(q)+c(q)$, where $c(q)$ is the number of $+$ signs of $q$ that survived, as one checks by induction on the length of $q$ (a $-$ raises the height, and a $+$ raises $c$ by one and lowers the height by one exactly when it cancels); if no $+$ of $s$ survived then $c(q)=0$ for every prefix $q$, so $\#+(q)\le\#-(q)$ for every prefix, contradicting the failure of (C). Therefore (C) holds if and only if, in $w'$, the entry at $p$ is the last surviving $+$, and the claim follows.

*Good versus cogood for a removable node.* Let $X$ be a removable $i$-node of $\mu$ and $
u=\mu\setminus X$. By step 1.2 the words of $\mu$ and $
u$ differ exactly by the flip at the position of $X$, so step 2.1 gives: $X$ is the good $i$-node of $\mu$ if and only if $X$ is the cogood $i$-node of $
u$. Consequently, if $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$ and $X$ is the good $i$-node, then $\varphi_i(
u)>0$ with cogood node $X$, and $	ilde f_i(
u)=
u\cup X=\mu$.

*Removing the good node preserves restrictedness.* Let $\mu$ be $p$-restricted and let $A=(r,\mu_r)$ be its good $i$-node; we show that $\nu=\mu\setminus A$ is $p$-restricted. If $r\ge2$ and $\mu_{r-1}-\mu_r=p-1$, then $B:=(r-1,\mu_{r-1})$ is a removable node of $\mu$ (as $\mu_{r-1}>\mu_r$) with $\operatorname{res}(B)=\mu_{r-1}-(r-1)=\mu_r-r+p\equiv\mu_r-r=\operatorname{res}(A)$, so $B$ is a removable $i$-node above $A$ and hence occurs before $A$ in the $i$-word. Either some $-$ before $A$ survives, and then $A$ is not the first surviving $-$, or every $-$ before $A$ is eventually cancelled, in particular $B$; but a $+$ cancels $B$ only after cancelling every entry pushed after $B$, in particular the entry at $A$, so in that case $A$ is cancelled and does not survive; both alternatives contradict that $A$ is good. Hence $\mu_{r-1}-\mu_r\le p-2$, and then $\nu$ is $p$-restricted: deleting the last node of row $r$ leaves $(\mu_r-1)-\mu_{r+1}\le p-2<p$ and, if $r\ge2$, $\mu_{r-1}-(\mu_r-1)=(\mu_{r-1}-\mu_r)+1\le p-1<p$, while all other consecutive differences are unchanged.

*Adding the cogood node preserves restrictedness.* Let $\mu$ be $p$-restricted and let $B=(r,\mu_r+1)$ be its cogood $i$-node; we show that $\nu=\mu\cup B$ is $p$-restricted. Suppose first that $\mu_r-\mu_{r+1}=p-1$; then $D:=(r+1,\mu_{r+1}+1)$ is an addable $i$-node of $\mu$, because $\mu_r>\mu_{r+1}$ and $\operatorname{res}(D)=\mu_{r+1}-r\equiv\mu_r+1-r=\operatorname{res}(B)$; between $B$ and $D$ in the top-to-bottom order there is no $i$-node: the entries after $B$ in row $r$ do not exist, and the remaining $i$-node of row $r$ is the removable node $(r,\mu_r)$, whose residue is $\operatorname{res}(B)-1$, while the addable node of row $r+1$ is $D$ itself. Hence $B$ and $D$ are consecutive in the $i$-word, both with sign $+$. If the $+$ at $B$ survives, it leaves the stack empty, so the next entry, the $+$ at $D$, also survives and is later than $B$; if the $+$ at $B$ does not survive, then $B$ is not the cogood node. In both cases $B$ is not the last surviving $+$, contradicting that $B$ is cogood. Hence $\mu_r-\mu_{r+1}\le p-2$, and then $(\mu_r+1)-\mu_{r+1}\le p-1<p$, while $\mu_{r-1}-(\mu_r+1)=(\mu_{r-1}-\mu_r)-1<p$ for $r\ge2$ (no row above change is needed when $r=1$), and all other differences are unchanged; so $\nu$ is $p$-restricted.

*Good versus cogood for an addable node.* Let $Y$ be an addable $i$-node of $\mu$ and $
u:=\mu\cup Y$. The node $Y$ is removable in $
u$, and $\mu=
u\setminus Y$; applying step 3.1 to the pair $(
u,Y)$ gives: $Y$ is the good $i$-node of $
u$ if and only if $Y$ is the cogood $i$-node of $\mu$. Consequently, if $\varphi_i(\mu)>0$ and $Y$ is the cogood $i$-node, then $\varepsilon_i(
u)>0$ with good node $Y$, and $	ilde e_i(
u)=
u\setminus Y=\mu$.

*The inverse property.* Let $\mu,
u$ be $p$-restricted partitions. If $
u=	ilde e_i\mu$, then $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, $
u=\mu\setminus A$ for the good $i$-node $A$ of $\mu$, and step 3.1 gives that $A$ is the cogood $i$-node of $
u$, so that $	ilde f_i
u=
u\cup A=\mu$. Conversely, if $\mu=	ilde f_i
u$, then $\varphi_i(
u)>0$, $\mu=
u\cup B$ for the cogood $i$-node $B$ of $
u$, and step 4.1 gives that $B$ is the good $i$-node of $\mu$, so that $	ilde e_i\mu=\mu\setminus B=
u$. Hence $\mu=	ilde f_i
u\iff
u=	ilde e_i\mu$ for all $p$-restricted $\mu,
u$, both sides being false when the relevant node does not exist; and by steps 3.2 and 3.3 the operators map $p$-restricted partitions to $p$-restricted partitions.

*Conclusion.* By [F1] at most one good and at most one cogood $i$-node exist in each residue, so the partial operators are well defined; removing a node lowers the rank by one and adding a node raises it by one, so $\tilde e_i$ lowers and $\tilde f_i$ raises the rank by one; and by step 5.1 each operator is defined at exactly the images of the other, so they are mutual inverses on their domains. No module theory and no choice principle are used.

citations.quote: For $H\le G$, restriction forgets from $\mathbb Z[G]$ to $\mathbb Z[H]$. For a left $H$-module $M$, set $\operatorname{Ind}_H^G M=\mathbb Z[G]\otimes_{\mathbb Z[H]}M$ and $\operatorname{Coind}_H^G M=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z[H]}(\mathbb Z[G],M)$, with $G$ acting on the latter by $(g\varphi)(x)=\varphi(xg)$.
If $H\le G$ and a left (respectively right) coset transversal is supplied, then $\mathbb Z[G]$ is free as a right (respectively left) $\mathbb Z[H]$-module on it.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra and $M$ a finite-dimensional left
$A$-module.

- Its **radical** is
  $$   \operatorname{rad}(M)=J(A)M,   $$
  equivalently the intersection of the maximal submodules, by
  [[thm-module-radical-is-jacobson-radical-times-the-module]].

- Its **socle** $\operatorname{Soc}(M)$ is the sum of all simple submodules, as
  in [[def-socle-of-a-module]].

- Its **head** or **top** is the quotient
  $$   \operatorname{hd}(M):=M/\operatorname{rad}(M),   $$
  formed using [[def-quotient-module]].

- Its **Loewy series** is the descending radical filtration
  $$   M\supseteq \operatorname{rad}(M)\supseteq \operatorname{rad}^2(M)\supseteq\cdots   $$
  together with the corresponding semisimple layers
  $\operatorname{rad}^i(M)/\operatorname{rad}^{i+1}(M)$.

The simple subquotients appearing in the Loewy layers are simple in the sense
of [[def-simple-module]].

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting
$p$-modular system for $S_n$, so that $k$ is a splitting field of
characteristic $p$ for $S_n$ and all its subgroups
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). For a partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ let
$$S^\lambda_k=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z},\qquad R^\lambda=S^\lambda_k\cap(S^\lambda_k)^{\perp},\qquad D^\lambda=S^\lambda_k/R^\lambda$$
be the modular Specht quotient of
[[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]], defined using the reduced
integral tabloid form on $M^\lambda_k$.

1. **Simple heads.** If $\lambda$ is $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda\ne0$ is
   self-dual and absolutely irreducible, and it is the simple head of
   $S^\lambda_k$, whose unique maximal submodule is
   $R^\lambda=\operatorname{rad}(S^\lambda_k)$. If $\lambda$ is not
   $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda=0$.
2. **Pairwise inequivalent.** If $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ are both $p$-regular

splitting fields for $S_n$. The proof uses no averaging and no division by a

be the **dual Specht module**, with
$$D(\mu):=\operatorname{hd}\bigl(S(\mu)\bigr) =S(\mu)/\operatorname{rad}\bigl(S(\mu)\bigr)$$

Let $M\ne0$ be a finite-dimensional $kS_d$-module and consider the multiplication map $\varphi:kS_d\otimes_{kS_{d-1}}M\to M$, $\varphi(g\otimes m)=gm$, where $M$ is regarded as a $kS_{d-1}$-module by restriction. For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an
$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$
(dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis
the classes of $\{m_{st}:s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.

3. The **Murphy cell module**
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ is free
with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$
and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$
with coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$.

4. There is a unique $R$-bilinear **Murphy form** $G_\lambda$ on
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with
$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; it is
symmetric, associative in the sense
$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$.

5. The basis, the ideals, the cell law and the form are compatible with every
base change.

In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is finite free of rank
$f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$. No choice principle is used.

In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with
generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with
$T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]):

1. $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$; in particular $H_v(n)$ is
free of rank $n!$ over $A$;
2. for every $w\in S_n$ and every $1\le i\le n-1$,
$$T_wT_i=T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad T_wT_i=(v-1)T_w+v\,T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1,$$
where $\ell$ is the inversion length of $S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]); consequently the rule rewrites
every monomial in the generators as an $A$-linear combination of the $T_w$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $F$ be a field, $q=1\in F$, and let $H_{F,1}(S_n)$ be the specialization of
the generic type-A Hecke algebra at $v\mapsto1$, so that
$H_{F,1}(S_n)\cong F[S_n]$ with $T_w\mapsto w$
([[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]).
Then the Hecke theory of this page specializes as follows.

1. The Murphy elements $m_\mu=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w$ specialize to the row
   symmetrizers $\sum_{w\in S_\mu}w$, and the Murphy basis $\{m_{st}\}$ of
   $H_{F,1}(S_n)$ specializes to the Murphy basis of the group algebra
   $F[S_n]$ (the base change $\mathbb Z[S_n]\to F[S_n]$ of the integral Murphy
   basis).
2. For every $\lambda\vdash n$ the specialization of the page's Hecke Specht
   module $S^{\lambda}$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) is
   the ordinary Specht module in the Dipper-James convention:
   $S^{\lambda}_{q=1}\cong S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}$ as $F[S_n]$-modules, with
   the standard polytabloid basis ([[thm-standard-polytabloid-basis]]); the
   specialized cell form is the standard bilinear form on $S^{\lambda}$ whose
   radical defines the James quotient $D^{\lambda}$
   ([[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]]).
3. The quantum characteristic of $q=1$ is $e=\operatorname{char}(F)$ when
   $\operatorname{char}(F)>0$, and $e=\infty$ when
   $\operatorname{char}(F)=0$
   ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]); in
   characteristic $p>0$ a partition is $e$-regular exactly when it is
   $p$-regular. Hence $D^{\lambda}_{q=1}\ne0$ exactly for $p$-regular $\lambda$
   ([[thm-specht-radical-quotient-is-nonzero-exactly-for-p-regular-partitions]]),
   and for non-$p$-regular $\lambda$ one has
   $\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}=S^{\lambda}$. This matches the group-side
   classification
   [[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]] and the
   conjugate-sign dictionary
   [[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]].
   In characteristic $0$ the specialization is split semisimple and all Specht
   modules are irreducible.

boundaries.reason: The proposition concerns n ≥ r ≥ 1 and the weight-(1^r) idempotent with r ≥ 1, so no empty-rank case arises; a rank-zero Schur functor is outside the statement.

boundaries.evidence: Zero multiplicities and zero Hom spaces are the values transferred by step 2.1: a first-level factor whose label is not ℓ-restricted maps to zero under the exact functor f.
A single composition factor is handled by step 2.1: the exact functor maps it to a Hecke simple by [F4] or to zero, preserving its multiplicity, and the count starts at one.
The q = 1 specialization is step 2.2, including positive characteristic (ℓ = p); the statement also covers ℓ = ∞ in characteristic zero.
The extreme first-level weight spaces λ − α_i and the extreme good row are not special: step 1.1 keeps all summands of the first level and step 1.3 treats every good row, in particular the topmost.
The proof uses the fixed idempotent e of weight (1^r) (step 1.1) and a single composition series (step 2.1); no choice principle is used.

boundaries.reason: The proposition asserts three separate statements (the first-level identification, the Hom isomorphism, and the socle labels), not a biconditional, so this slot does not apply.
No converse direction is asserted by this proposition.

derivations.claim: Construct the lower-rank action directly over the given field. Put $M_0=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Lambda(n-1,r-1)}M^\alpha$ for $H(r-1)$. Length-additive parabolic coset bases give $M^{(\alpha,1)}\cong M^\alpha\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)$ by $x_\alpha h\otimes a\mapsto x_\alpha ha$. Thus the summands with last coordinate $1$ form $M_1\cong M_0\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)$. The functorial algebra homomorphism $f\mapsto f\otimes1$ embeds $S(n-1,r-1)$ into $\operatorname{End}_{H(r)}(M_1)$: the Hecke algebra $H(r)$ is free on its parabolic coset basis and contains the unit coset, so the map is injective. Extend these maps by zero to the remaining summands of $M$ and put $p=\sum_{\alpha_n=1}1_\alpha$. For every left $S(n,r)$-module $V$, $V^1=pV$ is therefore a natural $S(n-1,r-1)$-module. This supplies the lower-rank action without assuming that the first level is a sum of root-adjacent highest-weight spaces, and without adjoining a square root of the Hecke parameter. It agrees with the last-coordinate polynomial level of [F3].

Prove the Hom assertion algebraically. For $S=S(n,r)$ put $\overline W=Se\otimes_{eSe}eW$ and let $\varepsilon:\overline W\to W$ send $se\otimes w$ to $sw$. Its image is $SeW=W^{(e)}$, which is $W$ under the stated hypothesis. Applying $e$ identifies $e\varepsilon$ with the isomorphism $eSe\otimes_{eSe}eW\to eW$. Exactness of $e(-)$ therefore gives $eK=0$ for $K=\ker\varepsilon$. The exact sequence is $$0\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow\overline W   \xrightarrow{\varepsilon}W\longrightarrow0.$$ For any $S$-map $g:\overline W\to V$, its image $g(K)$ is an $S$-submodule killed by $e$, so it is contained in $V_{(e)}=0$. Thus $g$ factors uniquely through $W$. The adjunction then gives $\operatorname{Hom}_H(eW,eV)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(\overline W,V) \cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(W,V)$. This proves assertion 2, with the kernel and quotient in the correct direction.

Reconcile the corners for all $n\ge r$. Put $\omega_*=(1^{r-1},0^{n-r},1)$ and $e_*=1_{\omega_*}$. Both $M^\omega$ and $M^{\omega_*}$ are the regular module $H(r)$. Their fixed identity isomorphism gives block matrix units $u,v\in S(n,r)$ with $u=e_*ue$, $v=eve_*$, $uv=e_*$ and $vu=e$. Thus multiplication by $u$ gives a natural isomorphism $eV\to e_*V$, with inverse multiplication by $v$, and carries the standard regular corner action to the $e_*$ corner action. When $n=r$ these corners coincide. This explicitly supplies the natural corner identification instead of treating an idempotent with last coordinate $0$ as lying in the first level.

Construct a perfect Schur-contravariant form on the permutation-summand module $M$. On each distinguished coset basis $b_d=x_\alpha T_d$, put $ eta_\alpha(b_d,b_c)=\delta_{dc}q^{\ell(d)}$. The row generator cases are a same-row scalar $q$, or an adjacent length-increasing pair with $b_dT_i=b_c$ and $b_cT_i=q b_d+(q-1)b_c$, $\ell(c)=\ell(d)+1$. Their weighted diagonal matrices verify $ eta_\alpha(aT_i,b)= eta_\alpha(a,bT_i)$, so the forms are Hecke-contravariant and perfect. To prove Schur adjointness, work first in $A=\mathbb Z[Q,Q^{-1}]$. Length-additive cosets and [F4] give $	au(a^*b)=P_\alpha(Q) eta_\alpha(a,b)$ on $M_\alpha$, where $P_\alpha=\sum_{u\in S_\alpha}Q^{\ell(u)}$ is nonzero in $A$ with constant coefficient $1$. For $f=\varphi_{ST}:M_
u	o M_\mu$, $a=x_
u h$ and $b=x_\mu k$, membership in [F4] gives $m_{TS}x_\mu=P_\mu m_{TS}$ and $x_
u m_{TS}=P_
u m_{TS}$. Thus $$P_\mu eta_\mu(fa,b)=	au(h^*m_{TS}x_\mu k)=P_\mu	au(h^*m_{TS}k),\qquad P_

u(a,f^*b)=	au(h^*x_

The orthogonal sum $ eta= igoplus_\alpha eta_\alpha$ is therefore perfect and satisfies $ eta(sm,m')= eta(m,s^*m')$ for every actual Schur basis map and hence every $s\in S$. It identifies the left $S$-module $M$ with $M^\circ$. No Poincare factor is canceled in the given field, including at $q=1$.

Compute the first-level corner inside this induced action. The lower regular summand is $H(r-1)$, whose induction is $H(r-1)\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)=H(r)$, exactly the summand of type $\omega_*$. Its weight projection on $pV$ is $e_*$, so $f_{n-1,r-1}(V^1)=e_*V$. The lower corner operator given by left multiplication by $h\in H(r-1)$ induces left multiplication by the same $h$ on $H(r)$ under $a\otimes b\mapsto ab$. Thus every generator $T_1,\ldots,T_{r-2}$ acts exactly as its image in the upper regular corner, by equality of these explicit endomorphisms. The matrix units of step 2.1 identify the upper standard corner with this regular summand. They consequently give $f_{n-1,r-1}(V^1)\cong\operatorname{Res}f_{n,r}(V)$ on every module. This is an algebra-level calculation; it needs no generic semisimplicity or cellular/crystal label identification.

Determine the simple socle labels of $M$. Evaluation at $1$ in the regular summand gives $Se=\operatorname{Hom}_H(H,M)\cong M$ as a left $S$-module. Finite-dimensional star duality and [F4], together with step 2.2, give $$\operatorname{Hom}_S(L,M)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(M^\circ,L^\circ)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(Se,L)\cong eL$$ for every simple $L$. The last bijection evaluates a map at $e$, with inverse $v\mapsto(se\mapsto sv)$ for $v\in eL$. By [F2], $eL(\mu)$ is nonzero exactly for restricted $\mu$. Thus every simple submodule of $M$ has restricted label; for restricted $\lambda$, any nonzero map $L(\lambda)\to M$ is injective. The proof does not equate zero form quotients with zero actual module heads.

Transfer composition multiplicities by exactness, not by a Hom-space count. Apply $f_{n-1,r-1}$ to a finite composition series of $L_n(\lambda)^1$. By [F2] its factors become either zero or the pairwise nonisomorphic $D_{\mathrm M}^{\mu}$ for restricted $\mu$. Removing repeated terms of the resulting filtration therefore preserves the number of each surviving simple factor. Step 3.1 identifies its result with $\operatorname{Res}D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda}$, proving the stated equality. Assertion 3 is not used to claim that every composition factor survives; a socle statement alone would not justify that claim.

Prove the restricted-socle assertion over every original field. Applying $p$ to the injection $L_n(\lambda)\to M$ of step 3.2 embeds $L_n(\lambda)^1$ into $pM=M_1=M_0\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)$ with the actual lower action of step 1.1. The length-additive parabolic coset basis makes $H(r)$ free as a LEFT $H(r-1)$-module of rank $r$, so $M_1$ is $r$ copies of $M_0$ as a left lower Schur module. Apply steps 2.2 and 3.2 to $M_0\cong S(n-1,r-1)e_{\rm lower}$: its simple socle labels are exactly the surviving restricted labels. Every simple submodule of $L_n(\lambda)^1$ is a simple submodule of $M_1$, and therefore restricted. At degree zero $M_0=F$, with the unique empty label; at $n=r=1$ this is the convention $S(0,0)=F$. This proves assertion3, without adjoining a square root, using a splitting extension, assuming a quantum-hyperalgebra specialization, or requiring $\lambda_n=0$.

At $q=1$, [F5] identifies the corner algebras with group algebras. In ordinary regular labels the two modules are simultaneously twisted by sign and both partition labels are conjugated. Sign restricts along the group tower, is exact, and preserves the two compared multiplicities. This is the ordinary group interpretation, including characteristic $2$; it is not an untwisted identification of a restricted label with the same regular label. Steps 3.1, 1.2, 4.2 and 4.1 prove all the assertions.
