Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$, let $q\in R^{\times}$, let $d,n\ge0$ with $d\ge n$, and let $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Write $S:=S(d,n)=\mathrm{End}_H(M)$ for the type-A q-Schur algebra with $M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\mu}$ the direct sum of the permutation modules ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]) and let $\{\varphi_{ST}:\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n),\ S,T\in T_0(\lambda)\}$ be its cellular semistandard basis ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]] for the underlying Murphy elements and [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] for the standard basis along which this basis is defined). Put $\omega:=(1^n)\in\Lambda(d,n)$, the composition with $n$ parts equal to $1$ (legitimate because $d\ge n$), so that the Young subgroup $S_\omega$ is trivial and $m_\omega=1$; hence $$M^{\omega}=m_\omega H=H$$ is the regular right $H$-module. Let $t^{\omega}$ be the unique standard $\omega$-tableau, with entries $1,2,\dots,n$ down its single column; it is in particular the unique row-standard $\omega$-tableau whose entries increase down the column. Set $$e:=\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}\in S.$$

Then:

1. $e$ is the projection of $M$ onto the direct summand $M^{\omega}=H$ along the other summands $M^{\mu}$, $\mu\ne\omega$; in particular $e^2=e$ and $$eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})=\mathrm{End}_H(H),$$ via the algebra isomorphism $$\rho:H\longrightarrow eSe,\qquad h\longmapsto\rho_h,\qquad \rho_h(x):=hx,$$ left multiplication by $h$ on $M^{\omega}=H$ being a right $H$-module endomorphism. Here the isomorphism $eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})$ sends $efe$ to $f|_{M^{\omega}}$ and is inverted by extending an endomorphism of $M^{\omega}$ by zero on the other summands, and the identification $\mathrm{End}_H(H)\cong H$ sends an endomorphism to its value at $1$. By the construction of the semistandard basis elements $\varphi_{ST}$ (Mathas (4.13) with Corollaries 4.9 and 4.12; see the locator above), the diagonal element $\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}$ is exactly the endomorphism of $M$ that is the identity on $M^{\omega}$ and zero on all $M^{\mu}$ with $\mu\ne\omega$, which is the projection asserted above. 2. The **Schur functor** is $$F:\mathrm{mod}\text{-}S\longrightarrow\mathrm{mod}\text{-}H,\qquad F(X):=Xe=X\otimes_SSe,$$ with the right $H$-action transported along $\rho$, so that $(xe)\cdot h:=x\,\rho_h$ for $x\in X$, $h\in H$ ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]). It is exact and $R$-linear on morphisms: as a **left** $S$-module, $Se$ is the image of the left-$S$-linear projection $s\mapsto se$ on $S$, hence is a direct summand of the regular left module and is projective. Tensoring right $S$-modules with this left module is therefore exact. Equivalently, for a short exact sequence of right modules, an element $ye$ in the target lifts to $xe$ from any lift $x$ of $y$; kernels and injections are likewise preserved by the same idempotent projection. The bimodule corner action makes these maps right $H$-linear. The convention is fixed: the functor is $X\mapsto Xe$ on the right, and the left-module formula $X\mapsto eX$ is not used on this page.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital cellular $F$-algebra with
cellular basis $(C,\Lambda)$ over the finite poset $\Lambda$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For $\lambda\in\Lambda$
put $D^{\lambda}:=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$, where
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the radical of the cell form
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]). Then:

1. if $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ then $D^{\lambda}$ is an absolutely irreducible
   (absolutely simple) $A$-module: it is simple over $F$ and remains simple
   after every extension of scalars to a larger field;
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ D^{\lambda}\ne0\}$ is a complete set of
   pairwise non-isomorphic simple $A$-modules ([[def-simple-module]],
   [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]]);
3. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if the cell form
   $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda$ is not identically zero, if and only if
   $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}\ne C^{\lambda}$; and, when these equivalent
   conditions hold, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the unique maximal proper
   submodule and the Jacobson radical of $C^{\lambda}$, so $D^{\lambda}$ is its
   simple head. If the form is identically zero, the cell-form quotient
   $D^{\lambda}$ is zero; no assertion about the Jacobson radical or the actual
   head of $C^{\lambda}$ is made.

No semisimplicity of $A$ is assumed; the theorem is the Graham-Lehrer
classification and applies in particular to $A=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for every field
$F$ and every $q\in F^{\times}$.

Let $F$ have characteristic $p>0$, let $N\ge2$, and let $\mu=(\mu_1\ge\cdots\ge\mu_N\ge0)$ be a polynomial highest weight. Let $L_N(\mu)$ be the nonzero Schur Weyl-cell simple at $q=1$, regarded as a left module by star, with its canonical highest vector $v$. Put $a_i=\mu_i-\mu_{i+1}$. For every $1\le r\le s<N$, define $B(i,j)=j-i+\sum_{t=i}^j a_t$ and $C(i,j)=j-i+\sum_{t=i}^{j-1}a_t$, reduced modulo $p$ for zero tests. A matching is an injection $d$ with $x\le d(x)$; it need not preserve order between different sources. Call $J\subseteq(r,s]$ essential when no $t<u$ outside $J$ in $[r,s+1]$ admits a zero-$B$ matching $\{t\}\cup(J\cap(t,u))\to[t,u)$. Write $\varepsilon_a(r,s)$ for the number of essential sets.

The vectors $T_{r,s}(J)v$ constructed by the explicit integral coefficient recursion in the proof, indexed by essential $J$, form a basis of $L_N(\mu)_{\mu-\alpha_r-\cdots-\alpha_s}$. In particular this weight-space dimension is $\varepsilon_a(r,s)$, including dimension zero. The construction has integer-polynomial coefficients, and its positive-word pivots remain valid in every field of characteristic $p$.

Define a root $x$ to be normal in $[x,y]$ when $a_x\ne0$ and its demands $m>x$ with $B(x,m)=0$ admit an injection $z$ satisfying $x<z(m)\le m$ and $B(z(m),m)=0$. If $r$ is not normal set $\nu_a(r,s)=0$; otherwise let it be the number of $x\in[r,s]$ normal in $[x,s]$ with $C(r,x)=0$. Set $\varepsilon'_a(r,t)=\varepsilon_{a+\omega_t}(r,t)$, where only coordinate $t$ is increased by one. Then, as ordinary integers,
$$\varepsilon_a(r,s)=\nu_a(r,s)+\sum_{u=r+1}^s\varepsilon'_a(r,u-1)\nu_a(u,s).$$
No restrictedness condition is imposed on $\mu$ or on the shifted auxiliary highest weights.

For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an
$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$
(dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis
the classes of $\{m_{st}:s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.

3. The **Murphy cell module**
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ is free
with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$
and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$
with coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$.

4. There is a unique $R$-bilinear **Murphy form** $G_\lambda$ on
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with
$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; it is
symmetric, associative in the sense
$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$.

5. The basis, the ideals, the cell law and the form are compatible with every
base change.

In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is finite free of rank
$f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$. No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and write $\mu=\lambda'$, $L=\ell(w_\lambda)$ and $N=\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))$. Let $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with its DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$, the cell module $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ with its Murphy form $G_{\lambda'}$, and the sign automorphism $\theta$ be as in [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]], and let $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ be the $\theta$-twisted cell module of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]]. Then:

1. There is a base-change compatible isomorphism of right $H$-modules $$\Phi_\lambda\colon P(\lambda)\longrightarrow C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta,\qquad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda)=m_0,\quad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda h)=m_0\theta(h)\ \ (h\in H),$$ where $m_0$ is the class of $x_{\lambda'}$ in $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and the right side is computed with the ordinary action on $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and read in the twist; in particular $\Phi_\lambda(e_t)=m_0\theta(T_{d_{\lambda'}(t)})$ for $t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda')$. For a class $m\in C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and any lift $\widetilde m\in M(\lambda')$, the inverse is $\Phi_\lambda^{-1}(m)=q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\theta(\widetilde m)$, independently of the chosen lift.

2. With $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$ the transported form of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]] and $u_\lambda(q):=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}\in A^\times$, $$G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=u_\lambda(q)\,\beta_{P(\lambda)}(x,y)\qquad(x,y\in P(\lambda)),$$ over every commutative $R$ with $q\in R^\times$. No unnamed scalar and no potentially vanishing scalar occurs: $u_\lambda$ is the explicit unit $q^{N-L}$ in the fixed normalizations of this page.

3. Consequently $\Phi_\lambda$ maps the radical of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ onto the radical of $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$, the induced map between the quotients is an isomorphism, with the corresponding cell-form quotients $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, including the zero-quotient case. Over a field, when the quotients are nonzero they are the simple heads; when the forms are identically zero, the displayed quotients are zero and no assertion about the actual module heads is made. Over a PID with a chosen prime, the unit-scaled form identity preserves all divisibility submodules and their reductions. One also obtains $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$ with the exact position of the dual and the twist, separating same-shape duality from conjugate-sign transport. No choice principle is used.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $F$ be a
field of characteristic $p$. Let $\beta_F$ be the reduced integral tabloid
form on $M^\lambda_F=F\otimes_{\mathbb Z}M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$, with
orthonormal tabloid basis, and let
$$S^\lambda_F\subseteq M^\lambda_F,\qquad R^\lambda_F:=S^\lambda_F\cap(S^\lambda_F)^{\perp},\qquad D^\lambda_F:=S^\lambda_F/R^\lambda_F,$$
where $V^{\perp}=\{x\in M^\lambda_F:\beta_F(x,v)=0\text{ for all }v\in V\}$
([[def-integral-tabloid-bilinear-form-and-specht-gram-matrix]],
[[thm-james-submodule-theorem-over-an-arbitrary-field]]). Let $G_\lambda$ be
the Gram matrix of the integral tabloid form in the standard-polytabloid
basis of the integral Specht lattice $S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$, and let
$g_\lambda$ be the positive greatest common divisor of its entries
([[def-integral-specht-lattice-and-base-change]],
[[lem-specht-gram-gcd-detects-p-regularity]]). Write $G_\lambda\bmod p$ for
the entrywise image of $G_\lambda$ in $F$, a matrix with entries in $F$.
Then:

1. **Vanishing criterion.**
   $$D^\lambda_F=0\iff p\mid G_{ij}\text{ for all }i,j \iff p\mid g_\lambda\iff\lambda\text{ is not }p\text{-regular},$$
   and equivalently $D^\lambda_F\ne0$ if and only if $z_j(\lambda)<p$ for
   every $j\ge1$, where $z_j(\lambda)$ is the number of parts of $\lambda$
   equal to $j$.
2. **Dimension.** $\dim_FD^\lambda_F=\operatorname{rank}_F(G_\lambda\bmod p)$;
   this dimension is determined by $\lambda$ and $p$ alone, and it is
   positive exactly when $\lambda$ is $p$-regular.
3. **Structure when nonzero.** If $\lambda$ is $p$-regular, then
   $D^\lambda_F\ne0$ is the simple, self-dual and absolutely irreducible
   head of $S^\lambda_F$, and $R^\lambda_F$ is the unique maximal submodule
   of $S^\lambda_F$, equal to the module radical
   $\operatorname{rad}(S^\lambda_F)$.

For the $k$ of a splitting $p$-modular system $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ for $S_n$,
$D^\lambda_k$ is the modular Specht quotient $D^\lambda$ of
[[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]], so the criterion above
decides for which $\lambda$ that quotient vanishes. No simplicity of
$S^\lambda_F$ itself is asserted.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting
$p$-modular system for $S_n$, so that $k$ is a splitting field of
characteristic $p$ for $S_n$ and all its subgroups
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). For a partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ let
$$S^\lambda_k=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z},\qquad R^\lambda=S^\lambda_k\cap(S^\lambda_k)^{\perp},\qquad D^\lambda=S^\lambda_k/R^\lambda$$
be the modular Specht quotient of
[[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]], defined using the reduced
integral tabloid form on $M^\lambda_k$.

1. **Simple heads.** If $\lambda$ is $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda\ne0$ is
   self-dual and absolutely irreducible, and it is the simple head of
   $S^\lambda_k$, whose unique maximal submodule is
   $R^\lambda=\operatorname{rad}(S^\lambda_k)$. If $\lambda$ is not
   $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda=0$.
2. **Pairwise inequivalent.** If $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ are both $p$-regular
   and $D^\lambda\cong D^\mu$ as $k[S_n]$-modules, then $\lambda=\mu$.
3. **Complete set.** Every simple $k[S_n]$-module is isomorphic to $D^\lambda$
   for exactly one $p$-regular partition $\lambda\vdash n$. Equivalently, as
   $\lambda$ ranges over the $p$-regular partitions of $n$, the modules
   $D^\lambda$ form a complete set of representatives of the isomorphism
   classes of simple $k[S_n]$-modules; in particular the number of simple
   $k[S_n]$-modules equals the number of $p$-regular partitions of $n$.

No absolutely irreducible module outside the family $\{D^\lambda\}$ is
constructed, and the statement asserts nothing about fields that are not
splitting fields for $S_n$. The proof uses no averaging and no division by a
group order, and the case $n=0$ and characteristic $2$ are included.

Fix a prime $p$, an integer $n\ge0$, and a **splitting $p$-modular system**
$(K,\mathcal O,k)$ for $S_n$, so that $K$ and $k$ are splitting fields for
$S_n$ and its subgroups
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). Write

$$M^\lambda_k:=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z},\qquad S^\lambda_k:=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}\subseteq M^\lambda_k$$

for the base change of the integral tabloid module and Specht lattice; the
inclusion is the injective polytabloid-span inclusion of
[[def-integral-specht-lattice-and-base-change]], and $S^\lambda_k$ has the
images of the standard polytabloids as $k$-basis. Let
$\beta_k:M^\lambda_k\times M^\lambda_k\to k$ be the reduced integral tabloid
form, the unique $k$-bilinear form with orthonormal tabloid basis
([[def-integral-tabloid-bilinear-form-and-specht-gram-matrix]]); it is
symmetric, nondegenerate, and $S_n$-invariant.

For a $k$-subspace $V\subseteq M^\lambda_k$ put

$$V^{\perp}:=\{\,x\in M^\lambda_k:\beta_k(x,v)=0\text{ for all }v\in V\,\}.$$

The **form radical** of $S^\lambda_k$ is

$$R^\lambda:=S^\lambda_k\cap (S^\lambda_k)^{\perp},$$

and the **modular Specht quotient** (or James quotient) is

$$D^\lambda:=S^\lambda_k/R^\lambda .$$

The quotient is a $k[S_n]$-module and may be zero. Its dimension is the
$p$-rank of the integral Gram matrix: if $G_\lambda$ is the Gram matrix of
$\beta$ in the standard-polytabloid basis and $\overline{G_\lambda}$ its
reduction modulo $p$, i.e. the matrix of $\beta_k$ in the standard basis of
$S^\lambda_k$, then

$$\dim_kD^\lambda=\operatorname{rank}_k\overline{G_\lambda} =\operatorname{rank}_k(G_\lambda\bmod p).$$

Everything is defined by scalar extension: $S^\lambda_k$ and $\beta_k$ are
determined by $\lambda$ and $k$, and no choice of lifts of elements of
$S^\lambda_k$ enters. $R^\lambda$ is a **form radical**, and is an
$S_n$-submodule; the identification of $R^\lambda$ with the module radical
$\operatorname{rad}(S^\lambda_k)=J(k[S_n])S^\lambda_k$
([[def-module-radical-socle-head-and-loewy-series]]) is a later consequence,
asserted only when $D^\lambda\ne0$. In particular no simplicity of
$D^\lambda$ is claimed here.

In the notation of
[[thm-normal-node-composition-multiplicities-under-residue-restriction]], let
$B$ be an addable $i$-node of the $p$-restricted partition $\mu$ such that
$\nu=\mu\cup B$ is again $p$-restricted, and let $F_i$ be the residue-summand
induction functor of
[[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]]. Then
$$[\,F_iD(\mu):D(\nu)\,]=0$$
if $B$ is not a conormal $i$-node of $\mu$, and
$$[\,F_iD(\mu):D(\nu)\,]=\#\{B':\ B'\ \text{conormal }i\text{-node of }\mu\text{ weakly above }B\}$$
(counting $B$ itself) if $B$ is conormal. The dual Specht-to-induction Hom
criterion (Kleshchev survey Theorem 11.7(i), Brundan 1998 Theorem 2.5 dual
form) is a distinct statement and is not asserted here.

Let $p>0$ and let $\mu$ be a $p$-restricted partition, so that
$\mu_i-\mu_{i+1}<p$ for all $i\ge1$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A node $(r,c)$ of
the Young diagram $[\mu]$ is an **$i$-node** if its residue
$$\operatorname{res}(r,c):=c-r\bmod p$$
equals $i\in\mathbb Z/p$; the $i$-nodes of $\mu$ are its addable and removable
nodes of residue $i$
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]).

**The reduced $i$-signature.** Fix $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and list the $i$-nodes
of $\mu$ as $A_1,\dots,A_n$ from top to bottom, that is, in increasing row
index and, for equal row index, in increasing column index. Form the word
$\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m=+$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m=-$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r<s$, $\sigma_r=-$,
$\sigma_s=+$ and $\sigma_{r+1}=\dots=\sigma_{s-1}=0$, replace $\sigma_r$ and
$\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$. The
resulting **reduced $i$-signature** has the form $+\cdots+- \cdots-$ with the
zeros deleted, and the nodes attached to its signs are:

- the **normal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the removable nodes corresponding to
  the $-$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **good $i$-node** is the topmost (first listed) of the normal $i$-nodes;
- the **conormal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the addable nodes corresponding to
  the $+$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **cogood $i$-node** is the bottommost (last listed) of the conormal
  $i$-nodes.

Write $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ and $\varphi_i(\mu)$ for the numbers of normal and
of conormal $i$-nodes of $\mu$; the good $i$-node exists exactly when
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, and the cogood $i$-node exactly when
$\varphi_i(\mu)>0$. At most one good and at most one cogood $i$-node occur,
for each residue.

**Well-definedness.** Each reduction step deletes two nonzero entries, so any
sequence of steps terminates after at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ steps, and in
the resulting word no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$: otherwise, take two
nonzero entries that are consecutive among the nonzero entries of the current
word and are ordered $-$, $+$; all entries strictly between them are $0$ by
the choice, so the pair would still be reducible. Hence, after deleting the zero entries, a terminal word is
$+^a-^b$ for some $a,b\ge0$; cancelled positions remain in their original
places and need not form a contiguous block. The terminal word does not depend on the
order in which reducible pairs are chosen: two reducible pairs cannot overlap
partially, because an endpoint of one pair lying strictly inside the other
would be a nonzero entry in a position that the other pair requires to be
$0$, and pairs sharing exactly one endpoint would similarly place a nonzero
entry strictly inside the other pair; so any two reducible pairs are either
disjoint (and the corresponding steps commute) or equal, there are no
critical pairs, and the rewriting relation is locally confluent. Uniqueness follows
by induction on the number of nonzero entries. A terminal word admits no
step. Otherwise, two distinct first steps commute and reach a common word
after one further step each. All these successor words have fewer nonzero
entries, so the induction hypothesis identifies their terminal words. Thus
any two reduction sequences have the same terminal word; in it the first surviving $-$ and the last surviving
$+$ are unique positions whenever they exist. Thus the reduced signature,
the sets of normal and conormal nodes, and the good and cogood nodes are well
defined. The empty partition has the unique addable node $(1,1)$, of residue $0$,
and no removable nodes. Its $0$-signature is $(+)$ and its other signatures
are empty. Thus $\varepsilon_i(\varnothing)=0$ for every $i$,
$\varphi_0(\varnothing)=1$, and $\varphi_i(\varnothing)=0$ for $i\ne0$.
It has no good node and its cogood $0$-node is $(1,1)$.

**Convention warning.** The residue $c-r$ used here is the negative of
Brundan's $\ell$-residue $r-c$, and a removable node of $\mu$ is normal here
exactly when its transposed node is normal in Brundan's sense for the
transpose partition $\mu'$; lists of addable and removable nodes, and the
signs of the residues, must never be silently mixed between the two
conventions
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ and let $L_1,\dots,L_n\in kS_n$
be the Jucys-Murphy elements $L_r=\sum_{s<r}(s,r)$ of the symmetric group
algebra ([[def-jucys-murphy-elements-of-the-symmetric-group-algebra]]). Recall
that they commute pairwise
([[cor-jucys-murphy-elements-commute-pairwise]]), and for $r\le n$ the
element $L_r$ lies in the subalgebra $kS_r\subseteq kS_n$ and therefore
commutes with $S_{r-1}$.

**(i) Primary idempotents.** In the commutative subalgebra
$k[L_1,\dots,L_n]\subseteq kS_n$ the minimal polynomial of each $L_r$ on the
regular module splits into linear factors $X-a$ with $a$ in the prime field
$\mathbb F_p\subseteq k$, and the commuting family admits the following
simultaneous primary decomposition. There are pairwise orthogonal idempotents
$P_{r,a}\in k[L_r]\subseteq k[L_1,\dots,L_n]$, indexed by $r\in\{1,\dots,n\}$
and $a\in\mathbb F_p$, with
$$\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_p}P_{r,a}=1,\qquad P_{r,a}P_{r,b}=\delta_{a,b}P_{r,a},$$
such that for every finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module $M$ the action of
$P_{r,a}$ on $M$ is the projection onto the generalized eigenspace
$M_{r,a}=\{m\in M:(L_r-a)^Nm=0\text{ for }N\gg0\}$. The $P_{r,a}$ for
different $r$ commute, and for each sequence $\mathbf i=(i_1,\dots,i_n)$
with entries in $\mathbb F_p$ the products
$$e(\mathbf i):=\prod_{r=1}^nP_{r,i_r}\ \in\ k[L_1,\dots,L_n]$$
are pairwise orthogonal idempotents with $\sum_{\mathbf i}e(\mathbf i)=1$ and
$e(\mathbf i)M=M_{\mathbf i}$, the simultaneous generalized weight space
$M_{\mathbf i}=\{m:(L_r-i_r)^Nm=0\ \forall r,\ N\gg0\}$. Every $P_{r,a}$ and
every $e(\mathbf i)$ is fixed by the antipode $g\mapsto g^{-1}$ of $kS_n$.

**(ii) Content sums and blocks.** The symmetric group $S_n$ permutes the
coordinates of sequences, and two sequences are called *equivalent* when they
differ by a permutation, i.e. when they have the same content (the same
multiset of entries of $\mathbb F_p$). Write $\mathcal C_n=(\mathbb F_p)^n/S_n$ for the set of content classes
(equivalently, multisets of $n$ residues). For $\alpha\in\mathcal C_n$ let
$I_\alpha$ be the set of sequences representing $\alpha$, and put
$$e_\alpha:=\sum_{\mathbf i\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf i)\ \in\ kS_n .$$
Each $e_\alpha$ is a central idempotent of $kS_n$, and distinct $e_\alpha$
are orthogonal; the nonzero $e_\alpha$ are exactly the primitive central
idempotents, that is the block idempotents of $kS_n$
([[def-p-blocks-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]), and every block
idempotent of $kS_n$ is of the form $e_\alpha$: this last identification of
the content sums with the blocks is the block theorem of Lyle-Mathas and
Brundan recorded as (2.41) in Kleshchev's survey (printed p. 11), with the
content of the block being the content of any of its partitions. The present
item proves the centrality, idempotency and orthogonality of the sums
$e_\alpha$ and then uses only those properties; primitivity and
exhaustiveness are recorded from the cited block theorem, not re-proved here.

**(iii) Residue-summand functors.** For a finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module
$M$, a residue $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and a content class
$\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}$, put
$$e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}:=\sum_{\mathbf j\in I_\alpha}e((\mathbf j,i)) \ =\ e_\alpha^{(n-1)}\,P_{n,i},$$
where $(\mathbf j,i)$ denotes concatenation, $e_\alpha^{(n-1)}=\sum_{\mathbf
j\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf j)$ is the content sum computed in $kS_{n-1}$ and
regarded in $kS_n$ through the inclusion $kS_{n-1}\subseteq kS_n$, and
$P_{n,i}\in k[L_n]$. Each $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$ is an idempotent of $kS_n$
commuting with $kS_{n-1}$, the family
$\{e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\}_{i\in\mathbb F_p,\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}}$ is a family of pairwise orthogonal
idempotents with $\sum_{i,\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=1$, and
$$E_iM:=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M =\bigoplus_{\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M$$
is a $kS_{n-1}$-submodule of the restricted module with
$$\operatorname{Res}^{S_n}_{S_{n-1}}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}E_iM .$$
Dually, for a finite-dimensional $kS_d$-module $M$ of content
$\alpha\in\mathcal C_d$, i.e. $M=e_\alpha^{(d)}M$, put
$$F_iM:=kS_{d+1}\,e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}M \qquad(i\in\mathbb Z/p),$$
with $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=e_\alpha^{(d)}P_{d+1,i}\in kS_{d+1}$; for a
general finite-dimensional $M$, with the sum indexed by $\alpha\in\mathcal C_d$, put
$F_iM:=\bigoplus_\alpha kS_{d+1}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}e_\alpha M$.
Then $\operatorname{Ind}^{S_{d+1}}_{S_d}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}F_iM$,
and all the functors $E_i,F_i$ are additive and exact, preserve
finite-dimensionality, and commute with contragredient duality, because the
projectors are fixed by the antipode. All statements hold at $p=2$; the
construction is choice-free.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra and $M$ a finite-dimensional left
$A$-module.

- Its **radical** is
  $$   \operatorname{rad}(M)=J(A)M,   $$
  equivalently the intersection of the maximal submodules, by
  [[thm-module-radical-is-jacobson-radical-times-the-module]].

- Its **socle** $\operatorname{Soc}(M)$ is the sum of all simple submodules, as
  in [[def-socle-of-a-module]].

- Its **head** or **top** is the quotient
  $$   \operatorname{hd}(M):=M/\operatorname{rad}(M),   $$
  formed using [[def-quotient-module]].

- Its **Loewy series** is the descending radical filtration
  $$   M\supseteq \operatorname{rad}(M)\supseteq \operatorname{rad}^2(M)\supseteq\cdots   $$
  together with the corresponding semisimple layers
  $\operatorname{rad}^i(M)/\operatorname{rad}^{i+1}(M)$.

The simple subquotients appearing in the Loewy layers are simple in the sense
of [[def-simple-module]].

boundaries.evidence: For μ = ∅ the unique addable node (1,1) of residue 0 is conormal and cogood, φ_0 = 1, and the statement gives F_0k ≅ k = D(1); the empty partition is the base case and is covered by the uniform count of step 1.1.
A zero multiplicity never occurs under the hypothesis φ_i(μ) > 0: step 1.1 computes the value φ_i(μ) ≥ 1, and F_iD(μ) is nonzero as a direct summand of the induction of a nonzero module.
The minimal case φ_i(μ) = 1 gives multiplicity 1 with simple socle D(ν) and no middle factor; steps 1.1 and 2.1 cover it.
p = 2 is the calibration of step 2.2: μ = (1), φ_1 = 2, and F_1D(1) ≅ kS_2 has socle, head and total multiplicity 2 for the trivial simple D(1,1).
Socle and head are the two endpoints of the Loewy series of F_iD(μ); step 2.1 identifies both with D(ν) via self-duality, and step 3.1 records that no claim is made about the middle layers.
No choice is made: the cogood node is unique in its residue and F_i is fixed by the idempotent decomposition; the calibration of step 2.2 is an explicit finite computation.

boundaries.reason: The theorem states that the cogood node B gives a simple socle and head of F_iD(μ) with total multiplicity φ_i(μ); it is not a biconditional, so no forward implication is asserted.
No converse is asserted: the statement does not claim that a simple socle of F_iD(μ) forces B to be the cogood node, only the implication from the cogood node to the socle and head.

derivations.claim: We first establish the restriction endpoint locally. Work with left Schur modules through star. In tensor degree $m$, the word of $m_\alpha T_w$ has $j$th letter the row containing $j$ in $t^\alpha w$; at regular type it is $jw^{-1}$, with zero-multiplicity labels omitted. Over $K=F(t)$ the evaluations $g^{\otimes m}$ span the tensor Schur algebra: a functional killing them gives a polynomial zero on invertible matrices; multiplication by $\det$ and the infinite-field polynomial identity force that polynomial to be zero. Schur simples are therefore simple polynomial $\mathrm{GL}_N$ modules. The canonical shape/type diagonal is its permutation-summand projection, whose square gives canonical form value one. Semistandard column strictness bounds entries at most $k$ by the first $k$ rows, so all weights are dominated by the highest weight $\xi$ and the highest space is $Kv$. Integer torus characters, rather than Lie eigenvalues modulo $p$, distinguish these weights.

Gaussian factorization $g=u^-tu^+$ on the big cell shows that negative coefficient operators on $v$ span its simple module: a functional killing them kills $gv$ on that open set and hence everywhere by polynomial identity. Similarly, positive coefficient operators detect every nonzero vector $x$ of weight $\xi-\Gamma$. If every positive highest coefficient vanished, the highest coefficient of $gx$ would vanish on the big cell, because negative operators cannot raise any weight to $\xi$; it would then vanish on the orbit of $x$, which spans the simple and contains $v$. All coefficient operators have integral tensor replacement matrices, and the ranks and Hom kernels of finite matrices preserve extension from $F$ to $K$. These arguments consequently descend to $F$.

Let $\xi_N=0$, $l=N-1$, and let $M$ be the full last-coordinate-one subspace of $L_N(\xi)$. A primitive vector means one killed by every nonconstant coefficient of the upper Levi unipotent group, not merely by its Lie generators. Factor the full upper group as $V U_l^+$, where $V$ has only the last column above the diagonal nontrivial. A positive test of a Levi-primitive vector acts only through $V$, since the right-hand nonconstant Levi coefficients kill it. Raising last coordinate $1$ to highest coordinate $0$ requires a $V$ monomial of degree exactly one. Positive detection therefore gives $E_{rN}x=cv\ne0$ for some $r$. Hence $\operatorname{wt}(x)=\xi-\beta_r$, where $\beta_r=\alpha_r+\cdots+\alpha_l$, even when the initial first-level deficit was arbitrary. On that primitive weight space $x\mapsto E_{rN}x$ is injective by the same detection argument, so its dimension is at most one.

Put $a_j=\xi_j-\xi_{j+1}$ and use $B(r,s)=s-r+\sum_{j=r}^s a_j$ and $C(r,s)=s-r+\sum_{j=r}^{s-1}a_j$. For nonempty $I$, the canonical $Q(I)$ kills a primitive vector: if $b=\min I$, its ascending-prefix letter $e_{b-1}$ commutes past the remaining ascending letters, whose indices exceed $b$, and becomes a rightmost Levi letter with $b-1<l$. Expand a nonzero primitive vector of weight $\xi-\beta_r$ in the essential $T$ basis and select the largest hat among its nonzero coefficients. The triangular pivot isolates a nonzero term. That hat cannot be nonempty, since its $Q$ test would annihilate the vector. Distinct essential hats therefore leave exactly one essential set with empty hat. Empty is linked precisely to a regular set, and the essential-regular matching theorem says such a set exists precisely when $r$ is normal. This proves necessity of normality.

Conversely, for normal $r$ let $R_r=\{s\in(r,l]:B(r,s)=0\}$ and choose its compensation $f$ with $r<f(s)\le s$ and $B(f(s),s)=0$. Put $D=f(R_r)$. The inverse matching makes $D$ regular, so its hat is empty. The matched norm is $\Xi_{r,l}(D)=\prod_{s\in[r,l]\setminus R_r}B(r,s)\ne0$: $B(r,r)=a_r\ne0$, and $R_r$ removes exactly the other zero factors. Thus $T_{r,l}(D)v$ is nonzero, and the maximal-hat assertion gives $h(I,D)=0$ for every nonempty $I$. For $r\le j<l$, every positive test of $e_jT(D)v$ has grade $\beta_r-\alpha_j$. Expanding its root matrices into simple words and appending the rightmost $e_j$ gives full words with nonempty canonical $Q$ index, since $e_j$ acts before $e_{j+1}$. All highest coefficients vanish, so positive detection gives $e_jT(D)v=0$. For $j<r$ the target weight is outside dominance below $\xi$ and is zero. A nonconstant Levi coefficient whose weight is not bounded by $\beta_r$ likewise has zero target. At a weight bounded by $\beta_r$, root-variable exponents are at most one, so the coefficient is a product of positive root matrices, each an iterated simple-root commutator; its rightmost root kills the vector. This proves full group primitivity. The primitive line at $\xi-\beta_r$ is consequently one-dimensional exactly at normal $r$, and we denote any nonzero vector on it by $v_r$.

We separate primitive labels integrally, including $p=2$. In tensor degree $b$ for Levi rank $l$, put $H_a=E_{aa}$ and define $\binom{H_a}{2}$ to act on a weight $\zeta$ by the integer $\binom{\zeta_a}{2}$ reduced in $F$. Concretely it is $\sum_{x<y}E_{aa}^{(x)}E_{aa}^{(y)}$, with no division by $2$ in $F$. The tensor action $Z_b$ of the group central transposition sum $z_b=\sum_{x<y}(x,y)$ satisfies the exact integer identity $Z_b=\sum_a\binom{H_a}{2}+\sum_{a<c}(E_{ac}E_{ca}-H_a)$. The equal-position part of $E_{ac}E_{ca}$ is $H_a$; after subtracting it, the terms are exactly the two swaps of unequal labels. The diagonal terms count equal-label pairs. Since $z_b$ commutes with the position group and every Schur endomorphism, this operator belongs to the Schur algebra and is central.

On a primitive vector of dominant weight $\zeta$, $E_{ac}$ kills it for $a<c$, so $E_{ac}E_{ca}$ acts by $H_a-H_c$. Therefore $Z_b$ has scalar $\kappa(\zeta)=\sum_a\binom{\zeta_a}{2}-\sum_c(c-1)\zeta_c=\sum_{(c,j)\in[\zeta]}(j-c)$. The binomial here is the actual diagonal weight operator of step 6.1. Centrality makes this scalar constant on the cyclic module generated by the vector. For first-level $\zeta_r=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_l)-\epsilon_r$, it is $\kappa(\zeta_r)=\kappa(\xi)- (\xi_r-r)$, so $\kappa(\zeta_t)-\kappa(\zeta_r)=-C(t,r)$. Thus the cyclic Levi module $\Psi_r$ generated by $v_r$ cannot contain another primitive $v_t$ when $C(t,r)\ne0$. Equality of the scalars alone does not prove simplicity; we treat it explicitly next.

Suppose $t<r$ are normal and $C(t,r)=0$. Choose $D$ for the demands of $r$ as in step 5.1. For $w\ge r$, $B(t,w)=B(r,w)$, and $B(t,r)=a_r
e0$. The demands of $t$ split into $Y=\{y\in(t,r):B(t,y)=0\}$ and $R_r$. Compensation for $Y$, inherited from normality of $t$, has image $E$ below $r$. Since $B(t,r-1)=C(t,r)-1=-1
e0$, all those targets and $E$ lie at most $r-2$. Combining their matching with $D$ gives compensation for every demand of $t$, so choose $v_t=T_{t,l}(E\cup D)v$ and $v_r=T_{r,l}(D)v$. For each $e\in E$ its matched $y$ gives $B(e,y)=B(t,y)=0$, hence $C(t,e)=0$. If $E
e\varnothing$ and $e=\max E$, then $C(e,r)=C(t,r)-C(t,e)=0$.

Splitting (P) gives $T_{t,r-1}(E)v_r=v_t-T_{t,l}((E\setminus\{e\})\cup\{r\}\cup D)v-C(e,r)T_{t,l}(E\cup\{r\}\cup D)v$. The last term is zero. The middle term has a (Z) witness with endpoint $r-1$, outside its cuts because $E\le r-2$ and $D>r$. Removing matched source $e$ releases its zero-$B$ target $y_e$; assign $t$ to $y_e$ and retain the matching on $E\setminus\{e\}$. All distinct bounded targets are below $r-1$. Hence that term is zero as well. For $E=\varnothing$, (P) omits the middle term and its last coefficient is $C(t,r)=0$. In both cases $v_t=T_{t,r-1}(E)v_r\in\Psi_r$, without a field denominator.

The Gaussian argument on a cyclic module, without assuming simplicity, shows that $\Psi_r$ is spanned by negative Levi coefficients on $v_r$ and has weights at most $\zeta_r$. Any nonzero proper Schur submodule contains a simple Schur submodule and thus a primitive $v_t$ by step 3.1. Dominance gives $t\le r$. For $t=r$, its one-dimensional line is the generating line and would generate all of $\Psi_r$; thus a proper submodule has $t<r$, and the central scalar requires $C(t,r)=0$. Conversely, such an earlier normal $t$ gives a proper nonzero $\Psi_t\subset\Psi_r$ by step 9.1, since its weights are at most $\zeta_t<\zeta_r$. Consequently $\Psi_r$ is simple precisely when $r$ is normal with no earlier normal $t$ satisfying $C(t,r)=0$. All simple Schur submodules of $M$ are exactly these $\Psi_r$, each once: every simple has a primitive highest vector, and each primitive line has dimension one.

Now assume $\xi$ restricted. The root criterion is its physical signature criterion: $a_r\ne0$ identifies the removable node in row $r$; scanning $j>r$, a nonzero $a_j$ gives a removable push if $C(r,j)=0$ and an addable pop at row $j+1$ if $B(r,j)=0$. These events have the residue of row $r$; at $a_j=0$ the matching slot supplies and consumes itself and is neutral. For $0<a_j<p$, the two events are disjoint. The compensation-prefix inequalities are exactly survival of the initial push in the signature stack. Also $C(t,r)=(\xi_t-t)-(\xi_r-r)$ compares the residues. Thus the simple cyclic modules in step 10.1 are exactly at the good nodes. Their lower labels are restricted: removing row $r$ decreases $a_r$ by one and increases $a_{r-1}$ by one. The only failure, when $r>1$, would be $a_{r-1}=p-1$. Then $C(r-1,r)=0$, and $r-1$ is also normal, since its later demands are those of $r$, $B(r-1,r)=a_r\ne0$, and the compensation for $r$ is also valid for $r-1$. This contradicts goodness. Hence every Schur socle factor survives the restricted-label corner; no assertion is made about the other composition factors.

To transfer without a held generic classifier, for $\xi\vdash m$ choose $N=m+1$ and the regular composition $\omega=(1^{m-1},0,1)$, so $\xi_N=0$ even for columns. Compute the cell corner temporarily in its original right-module convention, then transport through star. Its permutation summand is $M^\omega=FS_m$, and its actual projection $e$ gives $eSe=FS_m$ via $\rho_h(x)=hx$. Type-$\omega$ tableaux correspond to standard tableaux by increasing relabeling $1,\ldots,m-1,N$ to $1,\ldots,m$. Their normalized map fibers are singleton, and evaluation at $1$ sends $\varphi_{st}$ to $m_{st}$. Higher ideals correspond as equality of corner basis spans. The Weyl weight projection keeps exactly these basis vectors; read its cell action using a fixed outer index of the same type and evaluate at $1$ to get the Murphy action. Thus $W^\zeta e\cong C_M(\zeta)$ with the actual same-shape normalization.

In the Schur cell product choose all four indices $a,s,t,b$ standard of type $\omega$. Evaluation at $1$ turns $\varphi_{as}\varphi_{tb}\equiv B_\zeta(w_s,w_t)\varphi_{ab}$ into $m_{as}m_{tb}\equiv B_\zeta(w_s,w_t)m_{ab}$, so the unique Murphy coefficient gives $B_\zeta(w_s,w_t)=G_\zeta(c_s,c_t)$. The factor is one. Since $e^*=e$, the Weyl splitting $W=We\oplus W(1-e)$ is orthogonal, giving $\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}(We)=\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}(W)e$, including zero corner forms. Projection is exact by lifting $ye$ through $xe$ and taking kernels fixed by $e$. Hence $L^\zeta e\cong C_M(\zeta)/\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}$. The actual $q=1$ form-unit bridge identifies it with $D^{\zeta'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$, nonzero exactly when $\zeta'$ is regular. Transporting these right-cell identities through star gives the corresponding left corners $eW^\zeta$ and $eL^\zeta$ used below. Their nonzero images are exactly the distinct absolutely simple restricted-label modules $D(\zeta)$, with the inverse group convention fixed by the nondegenerate quotient form.

Let $\pi_1$ be the sum of actual weight projections with last coordinate one, so $M=\pi_1L_N(\xi)$. The lower Schur orbit matrix $E_A$ embeds as $E_{\operatorname{diag}(A,1)}$; on each word with one $N$ it preserves that position and applies $E_A$ to the remaining ordered positions. Products agree and the lower identity is $\pi_1$, and transpose/star is respected. The lower regular projection of $\omega'=(1^{m-1},0)$ maps to $e$. On the coset-word convention of step 1.1, $\rho'_h$ acts by label permutation $h^{-1}$ on the used lower labels, fixing $N$, identically to $\rho_h$ for the subgroup fixing the last entry of $S_m$. Thus, in the left convention, $e'M=eL_N(\xi)\downarrow_{S_{m-1}}$. Write $S_L=S(N-1,m-1)$ for this lower Schur algebra; every socle and corner lift of $M$ below is over $S_L$. The inverse/star equivalence passes between right and left modules and commutes with this embedding, restriction and sign; the ordinary simple labels are fixed by their nondegenerate invariant quotient forms. No self-duality of a degenerate Specht module is assumed.

Socle preservation requires more than exactness. By step 11.1 every Schur socle simple of $M$ survives $e'$. A nonzero Schur submodule killed by $e'$ would contain a simple submodule inside that socle, whose corner is nonzero, a contradiction. Now a group-simple injection $j:D\to e'M$ corresponds to $S_Le'\otimes_{e'S_Le'}D\to M$, $se'\otimes x\mapsto sj(x)$, $s\in S_L$. Its image $I$ is generated by its corner $e'I=j(D)$. A proper Schur submodule $J$ of $I$ has either $e'J=0$, excluded by the no-killed-submodule property, or $e'J=e'I$, which generates $I$ and forces $J=I$. Thus $I$ is simple. Every group-simple corner submodule lifts to an actual Schur simple submodule, and conversely every surviving Schur simple has simple corner. Exactness on the semisimple sum, distinct labels and the one-dimensional primitive lines yield $\operatorname{soc}_{FS_{m-1}}(e'M)=e'\operatorname{soc}_{S_L} M$, multiplicity-free with exactly the good-deletion labels. The unused coordinate includes columns and $m=1$, whose lower degree-zero corner is $F$.

The group central $z_m$ acts on $D(\xi)$ by $\kappa(\xi)$, since its tensor action is step 6.1 and its regular-summand action is $\rho_{z_m}$; right multiplication equals left multiplication for this central element. On the good lower label it acts by $\kappa(\xi-A)$. Therefore $L_m=z_m-z_{m-1}$ has scalar $\operatorname{res}(A)$ on that simple submodule, with the restricted convention $c-r$. Primary projection selects just that residue, and socles respect the actual direct sum. We obtain $\operatorname{soc}E_iD(\xi)=D(\xi-A_i)$ when $\varepsilon_i(\xi)>0$, and zero otherwise. In the latter case $E_iD(\xi)=0$, since a nonzero finite-dimensional module contains a simple submodule.

The invariant nondegenerate quotient form makes $D(\xi)$ self-dual. A primary polynomial projector in $L_m$ is self-adjoint, since the inverse involution fixes $L_m$, so its summand has a restricted nondegenerate invariant form. Its head is therefore dual to its simple socle and is the same simple. Thus for every restricted $\eta,\tau$ of consecutive degrees, $\dim_F\operatorname{Hom}(E_iD(\eta),D(\tau))$ is one if $\varepsilon_i(\eta)>0$ and $\eta-\operatorname{good}_i(\eta)=\tau$, and zero otherwise. The scalar endomorphism ring is $F$ by absolute simplicity. This all-pairs criterion includes the zero case and all initially possible primitive weights; it does not discard middle composition factors.

We justify the needed functor interfaces locally. In $\mathbb ZS_n$ the Jucys identity is $\prod_{r=1}^n(u+L_r)=\sum_{g\in S_n}u^{\#\operatorname{cycles}(g)}g$. Induct on $n$: choosing $u$ leaves $n$ fixed, and choosing $(a,n)$ inserts it next to $a$ in a cycle, bijectively covering the non-fixed permutations. Hence each elementary symmetric JM coefficient is central over every field. On a simultaneous primary tuple these operators have generalized eigenvalues equal to its elementary symmetric residue coefficients; nilpotence follows by expanding a polynomial in the commuting nilpotent differences. Distinct residue multisets have distinct coefficient tuples, since their monic products of prime-field linear factors retain multiplicities uniquely even in characteristic $p$. For each elementary symmetric operator, construct its univariate primary projectors by the same polynomial CRT construction as in [F5], then multiply these commuting projectors. This gives the content projector equal to the sum of tuple projectors of that content. This proves content centrality without factorial division, position-dependent symmetric-polynomial claims, or content-block primitivity. The projectors are inverse-fixed. For an input in content $\alpha$, induction projection by right $e_\alpha P_{d+1,i}$ is the same as right $P_{d+1,i}$, because $ge_\alpha\otimes x=g\otimes e_\alpha x$. An absolutely simple $D(\mu)$ lies in exactly one of these central contents, since their scalar idempotents are orthogonal and sum to one; denote it by $\alpha$. Thus these interfaces agree with the actual functor definition.

Put $G=S_{d+1}$, $H=S_d$, and let $E_H:FG\to FH$ truncate group coefficients. For left modules the natural Frobenius map is $\Phi(g\otimes x)(y)=E_H(yg)x$, with coinduction action $(a q)(y)=q(ya)$. It is balanced and $G$-linear by $E_H(hz)=hE_H(z)$ and $E_H(zh)=E_H(z)h$. For a left-coset transversal $T$ of $G/H$, its inverse is $\Psi(q)=\sum_{r\in T}r\otimes q(r^{-1})$. The right cosets $Hr^{-1}$ partition $G$, so evaluation at $y$ has exactly the term $yr\in H$ and returns $q(y)$. On $g\otimes x$ the unique term with $r^{-1}g\in H$ balances back to $g\otimes x$. These verify both identities and naturality with correct cosets and only finite choices.

Let $e=e_\alpha P_{d+1,i}$, commuting with $FH$ and inverse-fixed. For any such centralizer element, $E_H(eZ)=E_H(Ze)$: the coefficient at $h$ is the group coefficient trace $\tau(h^{-1}eZ)=\tau(h^{-1}Ze)$, by cyclicity and commuting $e$ with $h^{-1}$. Under $\Phi$, the value at one of right projection $R_e$ is consequently $q(e)$. If $f:N\to\operatorname{Coind}X$ is $G$-linear, $f(en)(1)=f(n)(e)$. Evaluation therefore identifies projected maps $N\to F_iX$ with $H$-maps $E_iN\to X$; conversely an $H$-map extends via $q_n(y)=h(yn)$. For $X=e_\alpha X$, every $H$-map already selects the matching content. Thus $\operatorname{Hom}_G(N,F_iX)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_H(E_iN,X)$ exactly, with no duality shift and no asserted equality of composition multiplicities.

The labelled signature inverse is local. Adding or removing a corner flips its $i$-sign, and the other boundary statuses that can change have residues $i\pm1$, not $i$ for $p\ge2$. In the stack reduction, flipping the last surviving plus gives the first surviving minus and conversely: before that position the minus stack is empty, and its distinguished minus survives exactly when every suffix prefix has at least as many minus pushes as plus pops, equivalent to no later plus surviving after the flip. Good removal preserves restrictedness by step 11.1. Cogood addition also does: its only possible new forbidden difference is $a_r=p-1$, in which case the addable node in row $r+1$ has the same residue, with no $i$-node between the two pluses. If the earlier plus survives, the later one also survives, contradicting that the earlier is cogood. Hence addition remains restricted and the inverse holds in both directions. In particular $B$ is cogood for $\mu$ exactly when it is good for $\nu=\mu\cup B$. No equality between $\varepsilon_i(\nu)$ and $\varphi_i(\mu)$ is used.

Apply step 20.1 with $N=D(\eta)$ and $X=D(\mu)$ for every restricted $\eta\vdash d+1$. By step 17.1 the resulting Hom space is one-dimensional precisely when $\eta-\operatorname{good}_i(\eta)=\mu$, and zero otherwise. Step 21.1 makes exactly one such label, namely $\nu=\mu\cup B$. The group simple classification covers every simple by these absolutely irreducible labels. The dimensions of all simple-to-module Hom spaces therefore identify the socle of $F_iD(\mu)$ as the single $D(\nu)$, with socle multiplicity one, excluding every other label.

Give $\operatorname{Ind}_H^G D(\mu)$ the invariant nondegenerate coset form $\beta(r\otimes x,s\otimes y)=\delta_{rs}\beta_\mu(x,y)$ on a finite left transversal. A group element permutes cosets and acts by $H$ on the fibers, proving invariance. Equivalently its value on general group representatives is $\beta_\mu(x,E_H(g^{-1}h)y)$. The projection $R_e$ is self-adjoint: moving it to the first argument gives $E_H(e^*g^{-1}h)$, which equals $E_H(g^{-1}he^*)$ by the trace calculation of step 20.1, and $e^*=e$. Thus $F_iD(\mu)$ is self-dual, and its head is the dual of its simple socle, namely $D(\nu)$ through the nondegenerate invariant quotient form. This proves both endpoints, including characteristic two.

For $d=0$, the empty partition has one conormal node $(1,1)$ of residue zero and $\varphi_0=1$. Induction from $S_0$ to $S_1$ is $F$, with $L_1=0$, so $F_0D(\varnothing)=D(1)=F$ has these endpoints; other residue functors are zero. ([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]]) define partial operators
$\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ for $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ by
$$\tilde e_i\mu:=\mu\setminus A\quad\text{if }\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0,$$
where $A$ is the good $i$-node of $\mu$
([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]), the
operator being undefined on $\mu$ when $\varepsilon_i(\mu)=0$; and
$$\tilde f_i\mu:=\mu\cup B\quad\text{if }\varphi_i(\mu)>0,$$
where $B$ is the cogood $i$-node of $\mu$, the operator being undefined on
$\mu$ when $\varphi_i(\mu)=0$. Then
$$\mu=\tilde f_i\nu\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\nu=\tilde e_i\mu$$
for all $p$-restricted $\mu,\nu$; in particular $\tilde e_i$ and $\tilde f_i$
are mutual inverses on their domains, each $\tilde e_i$ lowers the rank by one
and each $\tilde f_i$ raises the rank by one, and at most one good and at most
one cogood node exist in each residue. No module-theoretic statement is made
here: this item is pure combinatorics, and the identification of these
operators with the crystal operators of the level-one Fock space is a theorem
of the later Fock-space page, not an input here.

Let $p>0$ and let $\mu$ be a $p$-restricted partition, so that
$\mu_i-\mu_{i+1}<p$ for all $i\ge1$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A node $(r,c)$ of
the Young diagram $[\mu]$ is an **$i$-node** if its residue
$$\operatorname{res}(r,c):=c-r\bmod p$$
equals $i\in\mathbb Z/p$; the $i$-nodes of $\mu$ are its addable and removable
nodes of residue $i$
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]).

**The reduced $i$-signature.** Fix $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and list the $i$-nodes
of $\mu$ as $A_1,\dots,A_n$ from top to bottom, that is, in increasing row
index and, for equal row index, in increasing column index. Form the word
$\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m=+$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m=-$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r<s$, $\sigma_r=-$,
$\sigma_s=+$ and $\sigma_{r+1}=\dots=\sigma_{s-1}=0$, replace $\sigma_r$ and
$\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$. The
resulting **reduced $i$-signature** has the form $+\cdots+- \cdots-$ with the
zeros deleted, and the nodes attached to its signs are:

- the **normal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the removable nodes corresponding to
  the $-$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **good $i$-node** is the topmost (first listed) of the normal $i$-nodes;
- the **conormal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the addable nodes corresponding to
  the $+$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **cogood $i$-node** is the bottommost (last listed) of the conormal
  $i$-nodes.

Write $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ and $\varphi_i(\mu)$ for the numbers of normal and
of conormal $i$-nodes of $\mu$; the good $i$-node exists exactly when
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, and the cogood $i$-node exactly when
$\varphi_i(\mu)>0$. At most one good and at most one cogood $i$-node occur,
for each residue.

**Well-definedness.** Each reduction step deletes two nonzero entries, so any
sequence of steps terminates after at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ steps, and in
the resulting word no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$: otherwise, take two
nonzero entries that are consecutive among the nonzero entries of the current
word and are ordered $-$, $+$; all entries strictly between them are $0$ by
the choice, so the pair would still be reducible. Hence, after deleting the zero entries, a terminal word is
$+^a-^b$ for some $a,b\ge0$; cancelled positions remain in their original
places and need not form a contiguous block. The terminal word does not depend on the
order in which reducible pairs are chosen: two reducible pairs cannot overlap
partially, because an endpoint of one pair lying strictly inside the other
would be a nonzero entry in a position that the other pair requires to be
$0$, and pairs sharing exactly one endpoint would similarly place a nonzero
entry strictly inside the other pair; so any two reducible pairs are either
disjoint (and the corresponding steps commute) or equal, there are no
critical pairs, and the rewriting relation is locally confluent. Uniqueness follows
by induction on the number of nonzero entries. A terminal word admits no
step. Otherwise, two distinct first steps commute and reach a common word
after one further step each. All these successor words have fewer nonzero
entries, so the induction hypothesis identifies their terminal words. Thus
any two reduction sequences have the same terminal word; in it the first surviving $-$ and the last surviving
$+$ are unique positions whenever they exist. Thus the reduced signature,
the sets of normal and conormal nodes, and the good and cogood nodes are well
defined. The empty partition has the unique addable node $(1,1)$, of residue $0$,
and no removable nodes. Its $0$-signature is $(+)$ and its other signatures
are empty. Thus $\varepsilon_i(\varnothing)=0$ for every $i$,
$\varphi_0(\varnothing)=1$, and $\varphi_i(\varnothing)=0$ for $i\ne0$.
It has no good node and its cogood $0$-node is $(1,1)$.

**Convention warning.** The residue $c-r$ used here is the negative of
Brundan's $\ell$-residue $r-c$, and a removable node of $\mu$ is normal here
exactly when its transposed node is normal in Brundan's sense for the
transpose partition $\mu'$; lists of addable and removable nodes, and the
signs of the residues, must never be silently mixed between the two
conventions
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

On the set of $p$-restricted partitions
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]]) define partial operators
$\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ for $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ by
$$\tilde e_i\mu:=\mu\setminus A\quad\text{if }\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0,$$
where $A$ is the good $i$-node of $\mu$

operator being undefined on $\mu$ when $\varepsilon_i(\mu)=0$; and
$$\tilde f_i\mu:=\mu\cup B\quad\text{if }\varphi_i(\mu)>0,$$
where $B$ is the cogood $i$-node of $\mu$, the operator being undefined on
$\mu$ when $\varphi_i(\mu)=0$. Then
$$\mu=\tilde f_i\nu\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\nu=\tilde e_i\mu$$
for all $p$-restricted $\mu,\nu$; in particular $\tilde e_i$ and $\tilde f_i$
are mutual inverses on their domains, each $\tilde e_i$ lowers the rank by one
and each $\tilde f_i$ raises the rank by one, and at most one good and at most

here: this item is pure combinatorics, and the identification of these
operators with the crystal operators of the level-one Fock space is a theorem
of the later Fock-space page, not an input here.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$. Every $p$-restricted partition
$\mu$ of $d$ is obtained from the empty partition by $d$ successive cogood
additions: there are residues $i_1,\dots,i_d$ with
$$\mu=\tilde f_{i_d}\cdots\tilde f_{i_1}\varnothing;$$
equivalently, every $p$-restricted $\mu\ne\varnothing$ has at least one good
node, and successive good deletions carry $\mu$ to $\varnothing$
([[def-good-node-and-cogood-node-crystal-operators]],
[[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]). Hence, in
the graph whose vertices are the $p$-restricted partitions and whose edges
join $\nu$ to $\tilde f_i\nu$ for every $i$ for which the operator is
defined, the empty partition is the unique vertex of rank $0$ and every
vertex is reached from it; dually every vertex reaches the empty partition by
successive good deletions. The argument is choice-free.

derivations.claim: The $0$-nodes of $\varnothing$ and $(1)$. The empty partition has the single addable node $(1,1)$ of residue $c-r=0$, so its residue-$0$ word is $(+)$ and the cogood node is $(1,1)$, whence $\tilde f_0\varnothing=(1)$; the partition $(1)$ has the single removable node $(1,1)$ of residue $0$, so its residue-$0$ word is $(-)$ with good node $(1,1)$ and $\tilde e_0(1)=\varnothing$.

The $1$-nodes of $(1,1)$ and $(1,1,1)$. In $(1,1)$ the residue-$1$ nodes are the addable nodes $(1,2)$ (residue $2-1=1$) and $(3,1)$ (residue $1-3=-2\equiv1$), ordered $(1,2),(3,1)$ top to bottom; the word is $(+,+)$, the cogood node is the last surviving $+$, namely $(3,1)$, and $\tilde f_1(1,1)=(1,1,1)$, while adding $(1,2)$ would lead to $(2,1)$. In $(1,1,1)$ the residue-$1$ nodes are the addable node $(1,2)$ and the removable node $(3,1)$; the word $(+,-)$ is already reduced, so the surviving $+$ is $(1,2)$ and the surviving $-$ is $(3,1)$: the cogood node is $(1,2)$ with $\tilde f_1(1,1,1)=(2,1,1)$, and the good node is $(3,1)$ with $\tilde e_1(1,1,1)=(1,1)$, in agreement with the inverse property of [F2].

The $2$-nodes of $(1)$ and $(1,1)$. The residue-$2$ nodes of $(1)$: the addable node $(2,1)$ has residue $1-2=-1\equiv2$, and there is no other, so the word is $(+)$ with cogood node $(2,1)$ and $\tilde f_2(1)=(1,1)$. For $(1,1)$ the residue-$2$ node is the removable node $(2,1)$ (residue $1-2\equiv2$), the word is $(-)$, the good node is $(2,1)$ and $\tilde e_2(1,1)=(1)$.

The $1$-nodes of $(2,1,1)$ and the $2$-nodes of $(2,1,1)$ and $(3,1,1)$. In $(2,1,1)$ the residue-$1$ nodes are the removable nodes $(1,2)$ (residue $2-1=1$) and $(3,1)$ (residue $1-3\equiv1$), listed $(1,2),(3,1)$: the word $(-,-)$ is reduced, so the good node is the first surviving $-$, namely $(1,2)$, and $\tilde e_1(2,1,1)=(1,1,1)$. The residue-$2$ nodes of $(2,1,1)$ are the single addable node $(1,3)$ (residue $3-1=2$): the word is $(+)$ with cogood node $(1,3)$ and $\tilde f_2(2,1,1)=(3,1,1)$. In $(3,1,1)$ the residue-$2$ nodes are the removable node $(1,3)$ (residue $2$) and the interior node $(2,1)$, which is neither addable nor removable; the word is $(-)$ with good node $(1,3)$ and $\tilde e_2(3,1,1)=(2,1,1)$.

The path and its reverse. Step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.2 and step 2.2 exhibit, successively, $\varnothing\to(1)\to(1,1)\to(1,1,1)\to(2,1,1)\to(3,1,1)$ as cogood additions with residues $0,2,1,1,2$, and each reverse step as the deletion of the good node of the same residue; by [F2] this is exactly the assertion that each forward step is a cogood addition and each reverse step a good deletion, and the five residue labels match the displayed path.

All reduced signatures claimed in the example are the ones computed: $(-)$ for $(1)$ at $i=0$ in step 1.1, $(-)$ for $(1,1)$ at $i=2$ in step 2.1, $(+,+)$ for $(1,1)$ and $(+,-)$ for $(1,1,1)$ at $i=1$ in step 1.2, and $(-,-)$ for $(2,1,1)$ at $i=1$, $(+)$ for $(2,1,1)$ at $i=2$ and $(-)$ for $(3,1,1)$ at $i=2$ in step 2.2; in particular the signature $(+,-)$ shows that reduced signatures need not be multiplicity-free, and the path still exists as [F3] predicts.

partition of $d\ge1$; write $D(\mu)$ for the simple $kS_d$-module labelled by
$\mu$
([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]],
[[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]).
Let $A_i$ denote the good $i$-node of $\mu$, for those
$i\in\mathbb Z/p$ with $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$
([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]). Then
$$\operatorname{soc}_{S_{d-1}}\bigl(D(\mu){\downarrow}_{S_{d-1}}\bigr)=\bigoplus_{i:\,\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0}D(\mu\setminus A_i),$$
a multiplicity-free sum over distinct simple modules: distinct residues give

of $d$ and $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ with $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$; let $A$ be the good
$i$-node and $\nu=\mu\setminus A$
([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]). For the

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra and $M$ a finite-dimensional left
$A$-module.

- Its **radical** is
  $$   \operatorname{rad}(M)=J(A)M,   $$
  equivalently the intersection of the maximal submodules, by
  [[thm-module-radical-is-jacobson-radical-times-the-module]].

- Its **socle** $\operatorname{Soc}(M)$ is the sum of all simple submodules, as
  in [[def-socle-of-a-module]].

- Its **head** or **top** is the quotient
  $$   \operatorname{hd}(M):=M/\operatorname{rad}(M),   $$
  formed using [[def-quotient-module]].

- Its **Loewy series** is the descending radical filtration
  $$   M\supseteq \operatorname{rad}(M)\supseteq \operatorname{rad}^2(M)\supseteq\cdots   $$

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and $A$ a unital $R$-algebra
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) that is free as an $R$-module on a
finite set $C=\{c^{\lambda}_{st}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ s,t\in T(\lambda)\}$,
where $(\Lambda,\unrhd)$ is a finite poset ([[def-partial-order]]; its strict
order is written $\rhd$) and each $T(\lambda)$ is a finite set. For
$\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ be the $R$-submodule of $A$ spanned
by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$.

Then $(C,\Lambda)$ is a **cellular basis** of $A$, and $A$ is a **cellular
algebra**, if:

(i) the $R$-linear map $i:A\to A$ with $i(c^{\lambda}_{st})=c^{\lambda}_{ts}$
for all $\lambda,s,t$ is an algebra anti-automorphism of $A$, i.e. $i(ab)=i(b)i(a)$
and $i(1)=1$ (equivalently $i$ is an isomorphism of $A$ with the opposite
algebra; the displayed formula forces $i^2=\mathrm{id}$); and

(ii) for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$, every $t\in T(\lambda)$ and every $a\in A$
there exist $r_v\in R$ ($v\in T(\lambda)$) with
$$c^{\lambda}_{st}\,a\equiv\sum_{v\in T(\lambda)}r_v\,c^{\lambda}_{sv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}.$$

**Cell modules.** For $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $C^{\lambda}$ be the free
$R$-module with basis $\{c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_{tt}:t\in T(\lambda)\}$;
condition (ii) makes $C^{\lambda}$ a right $A$-module by
$c^{\lambda}_t a:=\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_v$ when
$c^{\lambda}_{tt}a\equiv\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_{tv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$, and
it makes $C^{\lambda}$ a left $A$-module via $i$, the left action being
$a\cdot c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_t\,i(a)$. Both actions are well defined on
the freely spanning basis elements by (ii): the coefficients $r_v$ are unique
because $C$ is an $R$-basis of $A$ and the quotient by $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ kills
exactly the basis elements indexed by strictly larger labels, while applying
the anti-automorphism (i) to (ii) gives the same triangularity for left
multiplication. The module $C^{\lambda}$ is the **(right) cell module** of
$\lambda$, and
$$A^{\unrhd\lambda}/A^{\rhd\lambda}\cong C^{\lambda}\otimes_R C^{\lambda}$$
via $c^{\lambda}_{st}+A^{\rhd\lambda}\mapsto c^{\lambda}_s\otimes c^{\lambda}_t$,
where $A^{\unrhd\lambda}$ is spanned by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with
$\mu\unrhd\lambda$. A cellular algebra may have several cellular bases.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital cellular $F$-algebra with
cellular basis $(C,\Lambda)$ over the finite poset $\Lambda$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For $\lambda\in\Lambda$
put $D^{\lambda}:=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$, where
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the radical of the cell form
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]). Then:

1. if $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ then $D^{\lambda}$ is an absolutely irreducible
   (absolutely simple) $A$-module: it is simple over $F$ and remains simple
   after every extension of scalars to a larger field;
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ D^{\lambda}\ne0\}$ is a complete set of
   pairwise non-isomorphic simple $A$-modules ([[def-simple-module]],
   [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]]);
3. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if the cell form
   $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda$ is not identically zero, if and only if
   $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}\ne C^{\lambda}$; and, when these equivalent
   conditions hold, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the unique maximal proper
   submodule and the Jacobson radical of $C^{\lambda}$, so $D^{\lambda}$ is its
   simple head. If the form is identically zero, the cell-form quotient
   $D^{\lambda}$ is zero; no assertion about the Jacobson radical or the actual
   head of $C^{\lambda}$ is made.

No semisimplicity of $A$ is assumed; the theorem is the Graham-Lehrer
classification and applies in particular to $A=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for every field
$F$ and every $q\in F^{\times}$.

derivations.claim: Extend only to $K=F(t)$. This field is infinite, and extension preserves the rank of every finite Gram matrix. A nonzero Schur cell-form quotient stays simple after this extension: in any field a vector outside its radical generates the entire cell module by the cellular rank-one action, and the same argument applies to the extended nonzero Gram form. No algebraic closure or infinite-choice step is required.

At $q=1$, identify $ igoplus _
u M^
u$ with the tensorword basis of $(K^N)^{\otimes m}, m=|\mu |$, by sending $m_
u T_{d}$ to the word whose $j$th letter is the row containing entry $j$ in the row-standard tableau $t^
u d$. This is the explicit right-coset/tensorword convention; for regular type and basis $d$, that letter is $j d^{-1}$ under right permutation notation. The symmetric-group action on tensor positions is transported through this map, so inverses in labels and right-position actions are fixed consistently. The symmetric group permutes the tensor positions. An endomorphism commuting with this permutation action has matrix coefficients constant on its orbits on pairs of words. Such orbits are indexed by nonnegative integer matrices $A=(A_{ab})$ with $\sum A_{ab}=m$, recording the number of positions with input $b$ and output $a$. Let $E_{A}$ be the matrix with entry 1 on that orbit and 0 elsewhere. The $E_{A}$ have disjoint support and form a basis of the endomorphism algebra. For a matrix $g$, $g^{\otimes m}=\sum _{A} (\prod _{ab} g_{ab}^{A_{ab}})E_{A}$. The transpose involution sends $E_{A}$ to $E_{A^T}$; it is precisely the $q=1$ Schur star (the corresponding semistandard Hom maps are transposes under the orthonormal tensorword/permutation forms).

Invertible-matrix evaluations span this Schur algebra over $K$. Indeed a linear functional annihilating all $g^{\otimes m}$ gives a polynomial $P(g)=\sum _{A} c_{A} g^A$ vanishing whenever $\det(g)\ne 0$. Then $P\det$ vanishes at every matrix over $K$. An elementary induction on the number of variables shows that a polynomial over an infinite field vanishing everywhere is zero: regard it as a polynomial in the last variable and use infinitely many values, then apply the induction to its coefficients. Thus $P\det=0$ as a polynomial, and the polynomial domain gives $P=0$, so all $c_{A}$ vanish. Finite-dimensional duality proves the spanning claim. Consequently the star-converted Schur simple is a simple rational left $\operatorname{GL}_N$-module, with the same submodules and composition multiplicities as the right Schur module.

The canonical semistandard tableau has weight $\mu$ and Schur form value 1. Indeed its diagonal Schur basis element is the projection onto the permutation summand $M^\mu $: the defining Hom map is the identity there and zero on the other summands. Its square is itself, so the defining cell-product coefficient, which is the canonical tableau norm, is 1. This argument uses the canonical diagonal projection only, not an idempotence assertion for all diagonal tableau elements. Every semistandard tableau weight $\nu$ is dominated by $\mu $: for each $k$, all entries $\le k$ occur in the first $k$ rows by column strictness, so there are at most $\mu _{1}+\cdots +\mu _{k}$ of them. The unique tableau of weight $\mu$ is the canonical one. Thus $L$ has highest weight $\mu$ with one-dimensional highest space $K v$, and its positive upper unipotent group fixes $v$: any nonconstant positive-root coefficient would have weight strictly above $\mu$. Torus weights are integer characters, distinct as Laurent monomials over $K$; no Lie-eigenvalue congruence substitutes for weight equality.

On the open set where leading principal minors are nonzero, Gaussian elimination gives $g=u^- d u^+$. The negative-unipotent coefficient operators on $v$ span $L$. To see this, let $W$ be their span and let $\ell$ annihilate $W$. Then $\ell (gv)=0$ on that open set because $u^+v=v$ and $dv$ is a scalar multiple of $v$. A polynomial matrix coefficient vanishing there vanishes identically by the same polynomial-identity argument, so $\ell$ annihilates the coefficient orbit of $v$ under all $\operatorname{GL}_{N}$. That orbit spans $L$ by simplicity. Hence $W=L$.

Positive coefficient operators detect every nonzero vector $x$ of weight $\mu -\gamma$. If they all had zero highest coefficient on $x$, the Gaussian factorization would imply that the highest coefficient of $gx$ was zero on the same open set: negative operators cannot raise a weight to $\mu$, and no weight exceeds $\mu$. The resulting polynomial identity would make that coefficient zero on the whole simple-module orbit of $x$, which spans $L$ and contains $v$, a contradiction. Thus some positive coefficient operator of weight $\gamma$ raises $x$ to a nonzero multiple of $v$.

For $\gamma =\alpha (r,s)$, every simple-root coefficient is 1. In a product expansion of a unipotent matrix, any monomial of total root weight $\gamma$ therefore has each root-variable exponent $0$ or $1$, and its roots are pairwise disjoint intervals covering $[r,s]$. They are exactly cut partitions of that interval. Put  $f_{a,b}=E_{b+1,a}, e_{i}=E_{i,i+1}, Y_{r,s}(U)=f_{r,u_{1}-1}f_{u_{1},u_{2}-1}\cdots f_{u_{k},s}$, for $U=\{u_{1}<\cdots <u_{k}\}\subset (r,s]$, with $Y(\varnothing )=f_{r,s}$. These words span the required negative coefficient space. Similarly the positive coefficient space is spanned by words using each $e_{r},\cdots ,e_{s}$ once. Root-matrix commutators expand every longer positive root into such simple words. Permutations of these simple letters are identified using $e_{i} e_{j}=e_{j} e_{i}$ for $|i-j|>1$; their relative orders on adjacent pairs determine the canonical representative  $Q_{r,s}(I)=e_{i_{k}}\cdots e_{i_{1}} \cdot \prod _{j\in [r,s]\setminus I}^{\mathrm{increasing}}e_{j}, I=\{i_{1}<\cdots <i_{k}\}\subset (r,s]$. Every word is carried to this representative by exchanging adjacent incomparable letters in the corresponding path partial order. Hence these $Q$ words span all positive tests at the interval weight. There are no divided powers greater than 1 or factorial denominators in this grade.

The actions and all commutator calculations below use $[E_{ab},E_{cd}]=\delta _{bc} E_{ad} -\delta _{da} E_{cb}, e_{i} v=0$, and $(E_{ii} -E_{i+1,i+1})v=a_{i} v$. They are integral matrix identities and apply to the actual Schur module. The construction descends from $K$ to $F$ because the resulting matrices have entries in $F$ and scalar extension preserves all ranks and linear relations.
